subsubtopic: SALES TAX-REQUEST GOVERNMENT REPLY TO QUEBEC'S PROPOSAL AS SOON AS POSSIBLE-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, I request the unanimous consent of the House to present a motion on a very important matter.
In view of the fact that the sales tax proposal in the recent federal budget is aimed at fostering an economic recovery in Canada and the creation of jobs for over a million unemployed; that the proposal made by the Quebec government to the federal government takes into account those two objectives without additional expense; and finally, that it is in the best interest of the federal government to improve the fate of the 340,000 unemployed in Quebec and in such vital sectors as textiles, footwear and furniture, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey):
That the Minister of Finance be required to reply as soon as possible to Quebec's proposal.

That the House urge the Minister of Finance to take the necessary measures so as to increase to $5,000 the personal basic exemption of Canadian residents.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT URGED TO AMEND PROPOSALS-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity under the provisions of Standing Order 43. Whereas the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) announced on October 20, 1977, in his so-called economic and fiscal statement an income tax reduction for certain taxpayers for the year 1978, and whereas the said tax reduction as stated in a letter dated March 28, 1978, was allegedly to be done "to provide a quick stimulus to the economy", and whereas the said tax reduction was only for the period of January and February, 1978, causing a great deal of additional problems for employers and employees, and whereas the present Minister of Finance in his budget of April 10, 1978, announced a reduction or cut in provincial sales taxes, where applicable, for a period of six months, alleging that it would "provide fresh stimulus for industrial growth", and whereas the number of unemployed persons in Canada continues to rise and is now far in excess of the one million mark, and whereas there is still a desperate need to remedy the unemployment situation forthwith and at the same time give greater incentive to Canadian industry by encouraging production and the purchase of Canadian goods, I would move, seconded by the hon. member for Palliser (Mr. Schumacher):
That the House of Commons urge the Minister of Finance and his colleagues to amend the budget proposals now before the House to include the following:
(1)	A reduction in personal income taxes for the entire year 1978 similar to that granted for January and February 1978, and;
(2)	Elimination or substantial reduction of federal sales taxes on all Canadian made and/or produced and/or processed goods to help provide both incentive to industry and to provide needed employment for Canadians.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. subsubtopic: SALES TAX-INQUIRY WHETHER GOVERNMENT INTENDS TO REPLY TO QUEBEC'S PROPOSAL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I had the opportunity to talk with Mr. Parizeau a few minutes ago and I told him that his counter-proposal was not acceptable in the present circumstances, that during the coming six months we would be willing to pay two cents on each item on which he intends to cut the sales tax. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, is the minister in a position to tell us whether, before bringing down the budget, he had had negotiations or discussions with the provinces with regard to the intentions of the government? speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I had occasion to visit most finance ministers and spoke to the other ones over the telephone over the three-week period prior to bringing down the budget. subsubtopic: SALES TAX-INQUIRY WHETHER GOVERNMENT INTENDS TO REPLY TO QUEBEC'S PROPOSAL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am speaking to a minister who has a good knowledge of the province of Quebec and its current rate of unemployment. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for the hon. member who represents, I understand, the city of L'Assomption where refrigerators are manufactured, there are obvious distinctions

made about those producers. Victoriaville is home to manufacturers of rowboats, pleasure boats and other similar products. I say that I am happy to contribute to the program of the Quebec government by paying 2 per cent for six months. subtopic: SALES TAX-INQUIRY WHETHER GOVERNMENT READY TO DISCUSS QUEBEC'S PROPOSAL
SALES TAX-INQUIRY WHETHER GOVERNMENT READY TO DISCUSS QUEBEC'S PROPOSAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hope we will be able to run our federal policy not in a spirit of confrontation with the province of Quebec but in a spirit of flexibility.
In view of the lay-offs in the textile, clothing, footwear and furniture industries in the province of Quebec and, as the hon. member for Joliette has pointed out a few moments ago, the high level of unemployment in Quebec, and in view of the fact that in his speech Monday night the Minister of Finance stated many times that his policy was a striking example of federal-provincial co-operation, is the federal government prepared not to forget the present real economic needs of the province of Quebec and of our fellow citizens, those of the textile, clothing, footwear and furniture industries, and to discuss seriously with the Quebec minister the proposals made yesterday?

subtopic: SALES TAX-INQUIRY WHETHER GOVERNMENT READY TO DISCUSS QUEBEC'S PROPOSAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I discussed the proposals very seriously during a three-week period with the provincial governments. Mr. Parizeau made no proposal to me along the lines of those he made yesterday, all the more as the sales tax cut applies to all other small businesses in Quebec, not only to those in that special area. Furthermore, the sales tax cut in the rest of Canada is going to help the Canadian people outside the province of Quebec to buy textile, footwear and furniture manufactured in Quebec. I think it is an extremely important item. Well, Mr. Speaker, we made some offers in good faith to the provincial governments. All the other governments had counterproposals to make; I even made adjustments to meet the particular situation in British Columbia and Saskatchewan, and at that time Mr. Parizeau did not mention any counterproposal. He listened kindly, politely, and he only made this proposal yesterday, after the other provinces had made their decision. What I said, and I say it again, is that we are prepared to pay for each of the items exempted under Mr. Parizeau's plan, namely 2 per cent for six months, and if he decides in future weeks or months to cut the sales tax on the other products to assist the other sectors of the Quebec economy which are also very

April 13, 1978

important, we shall be prepared to pay them the amount as promised.

subtopic: SALES TAX-INQUIRY WHETHER GOVERNMENT READY TO DISCUSS QUEBEC'S PROPOSAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 wish to ask a supplementary question.
I fully agree with the Minister of Finance that we must take into account the whole secondary industry in the province of Quebec, but in view of the fact that in that province the textile, furniture, footwear and clothing industries hold the highest percentage of lay-offs, could the minister tell the House if he is really prepared to examine more seriously Quebec's proposals in that light.

subtopic: SALES TAX-INQUIRY WHETHER GOVERNMENT READY TO DISCUSS QUEBEC'S PROPOSAL

On my part, I maintain my offer. My proposals involve tremendous support to the footwear, textile and clothing industries since they will prompt other Canadians to buy those products manufactured in Quebec; moreover, I think that if the Quebec government wants to help the other sectors, the money will remain available.

subtopic: VALUE OF CANADIAN DOLLAR-PEGGING WHEN U.S. DOLLAR STABILIZES
VALUE OF CANADIAN DOLLAR-PEGGING WHEN U.S. DOLLAR STABILIZES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. The Minister of State for Fitness and Amateur Sport was quoted on April 5 of this year as saying:
The federal government will move to fix the value of the Canadian dollar on the international money market once the U.S. dollar stabilizes.
Can the Prime Minister advise the House if that reflects government policy?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: VALUE OF CANADIAN DOLLAR-PEGGING WHEN U.S. DOLLAR STABILIZES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I will take notice of the quotation and verify its accuracy.

I have a supplementary question for the Minister of Finance. Can he now confirm that it is costing the Canadian taxpayer approximately $750,000 a day in interest charges, or an annual cost of $275 million and, if so, would he not agree it would be better that we use this kind of money to put Canadians to work and stimulate the domestic economy, rather than tossing it away on foreign speculators?

The hon. member should check his figures again, because the figures he

uses are completely false. We are not spending that much money.
How much?
I can give you the figures. It is a very complex formula.
Oh oh!

Tomorrow I will give hon. members the exact amount of money involved. I will look into that. The figure mentioned by the hon. member does not represent the cost, and I have checked it very carefully. The figure used by the leader of the hon. member's party is unbelievably out of range. I will be delighted to make a comparison tomorrow. It would be better for the leader of that party, who claims to be an economist, to use a little calculator.
I am sure the minister can agree that it is in the hundreds of millions of dollars, or at least a very substantial figure.
No.

When the Minister of Finance was looking after the foreign investment review legislation, we started a welcome-wagon process in Canada. In terms of the current balance of payments situation, our merchandise trade surplus is $2.9 billion; we are running a surplus on merchandise trade. But when you get to the service account and to what we are paying in interest and dividends to foreign ownership in Canada, that is when we find ourselves in a deficit position.
My question to the minister is this: Can we now expect some meaningful foreign investment legislation so that we can stop paying our absentee landlords these massive amounts and driving down the Canadian dollar?

Mr. Speaker, I am surprised an hon. member of a party that is always claiming there are not enough jobs being created in Canada would want to take measures to restrict the inflow of capital into Canada which would create jobs.

SALES TAX-EFFECT OF REDUCTION ON QUEBEC MUNICIPALITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is of course for the Minister of Finance. It is unfortunate that such a controversy would create even more division to reduce the harmony that should exist in Canada. In any event, I would like to ask the Minister of Finance if he considered, when he made his budget speech and as concerns the retail sales tax reduction that he suggested to stimulate the Canadian economy, what impact this policy will have on the income
April 13, 1978

of Quebec municipalities which get a very large part of their income from the reimbursement of the provincial sales tax?

subtopic: SALES TAX-EFFECT OF REDUCTION ON QUEBEC MUNICIPALITIES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this is a point that Mr. Parizeau raised in his statement yesterday during his press conference. He said in effect that the sales tax proposals would in no way affect the income of municipalities and that the provincial government would make the necessary adjustments.

subtopic: SALES TAX-EFFECT OF REDUCTION ON QUEBEC MUNICIPALITIES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, since the proposal of the Quebec finance minister will result in the complete removal of the provincial retail sales tax on the products of the textile, furniture and footwear industries and since this will apply over a period of 12 months instead of six months as announced by the Minister of Finance, can the minister tell the House if this delay, or this margin of six months was discussed with the Quebec finance minister and if this will result in a difference of compensation to be paid to the province of Quebec as provided in the budget speech?

subtopic: SALES TAX-EFFECT OF REDUCTION ON QUEBEC MUNICIPALITIES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we have amended our proposal to the provinces and this has allowed British Columbia, for instance, to apply a tax of 2 per cent instead of 3 per cent over a longer period, up to at least nine months. Our proposal was given some flexibility, as Mr. Parizeau was well aware.

subtopic: SALES TAX-EFFECT OF REDUCTION ON QUEBEC MUNICIPALITIES
speechtext: A supplementary Mr. Speaker. Since this is boiling down to a revenue battle between the federal government and the provinces, would the Minister of Finance consider reviewing having a fresh look at the possibility of subsidizing those tax reductions amounting to a discount for consumers which, as announced in the budget, is going to be paid from the taxpayers' money? Would the minister be prepared to study in depth the possibility of creating extra credit through the Bank of Canada, increasing the money supply since the minister's aim is to increase the consumers' purchasing power? I think this should be considered. Is the minister prepared to have this financial proposition studied by his officials to accommodate both the Canadian government and the provinces?

subtopic: SALES TAX-EFFECT OF REDUCTION ON QUEBEC MUNICIPALITIES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as soon as I entered politics in 1963 it was my pleasure to go into social credit theories, and I am now more convinced than ever that I was right to oppose them at this time. Therefore in 1978 I am still against them.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. We witnessed the dollar falling even further today, to 86.79 cents, having lost $30 million this morning in trying to defend the floating dollar. So far this month, $300 million has gone out.
Oral Questions
Would the minister try to give some stabilization to the market by indicating to the House what the government plans to borrow in the foreign markets? How much of their $11.5 billion total financial requirements will be raised in foreign markets?

Mr. Speaker, I stated the policy of the government in my budget statement on monetary policies, and I have nothing to add to it. Of course, when the time comes for the financing of cash requirements, the market will be informed of the form of borrwing we will be adopting at that time, and where.

A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Whether the Minister of Finance likes it or not, there is growing anxiety in the inernational market about this monetary policy which the minister says is so clear. In particular, last year it caused the Bank of Canada to buy 23 per cent of their total financial requirements at the federal level.
Would the minister indicate if they plan to cause the Bank of Canada to buy debt of the federal treasury to that extent this year and, if they do, does he not feel that will demoralize the international money market still further?
Mr. Speaker, the monetary policies are executed by the governor of the Bank of Canada, and when we decide to act we will make it public at that time.

Mr. Speaker, my final supplementary question to the Minister of Finance is based upon a report put out by Friedberg and Company Limited this month, in which they assess the monetary policy the minister appears to be so proud of and indicate that if the government persists in their approach, it will result in a 25 per cent devaluation in Canada, to be taken out with a falling dollar or inflation, or both.
In consequence of that type of a devaluation, would the minister not reconsider the statement he made to the House and indicate that he will at least take the matter up with the governor of the Bank of Canada with a view to having a saner monetary policy in this country.

Mr. Speaker, I should like the hon. member to tell the House and the country if he is for pegging the Canadian dollar at a certain level, and where. I am not about to speculate on that in the way the hon. member does.
Ask Jack Horner.
I am not about to speculate on those matters. The policy is well known, and the Canadian dollar is a floating dollar.

What does "Loose Lips" say?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Postmaster General. subsubtopic: MISHANDLING OF MAIL
speechtext:

April 13, 1978

I asked the Businessmen's Club yesterday if anyone in business could claim to have an error factor of only 1 per cent. If anyone can claim that, they are very good. It must be realized, too, that the consequences of a 1 per cent error factor may be a little more important in the Post Office than anywhere else. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, a supplementary question. subsubtopic: MISHANDLING OF MAIL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on that issue I answered quite clearly to my audience there was no question for the moment of refusing uncoded mail. As an illustration, Australia has a legal requirement that a letter must show the code if it is to be delivered. What I meant on that occasion is therefore that in the future we will have to try and standardize the way people send their mail. subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON DAIRY POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I am pleased to announce the broad outline for the 1978-79 dairy program. As of April 1, 1978, total market sharing quota remains unchanged for the dairy year ending March 31, 1979, for a total of 103.7 million hundredweights. The level of the federal subsidy paid on all industrial milk produced within Canadian requirements remains unchanged at $2.66 per hundredweight. The target price will be increased by 24 cents, to $12.42 per hundredweight. This will mean a five-cent increase in the support price of butter, to $1.27 per pound. The support price of skim milk powder also goes up by two cents, to 74 cents a pound.

The extra 24 cents, plus two other increases during the year, will raise returns to producers by a total of about 76 cents a hundredweight compared with what they got at the same time last year. That means a producer of 300,000 pounds annually will get an additional $2,300. However, let me remind the House that those increases are less than the present general rate of inflation and are needed to maintain producer incomes in the face of rising costs.
The direct levy on in-quota production is reduced to $ 1 per hundredweight, but every hundredweight of in-quota industrial milk and cream will be subject to a new contingency level of 20 cents, refundable to those producers who, at year end, have managed to keep their production within national requirements.
There will be a levy of $ 1 on every hundredweight of surplus cream diverted from fluid to industrial use. I should remind the House that this levy is equivalent to 20 cents per hundredweight on fluid shipments which, in fact, were subject to a 25 cents per hundredweight levy last year.
The over-quota levy will be raised by 50 cents, to $7.50 per hundredweight.
Some good news for those hon. members who have long been asking questions about the difficulties faced by Canada's cheese industry is the new level set for cheese imports. Total imports of cheese will not be allowed to exceed 45 million pounds over the dairy year, down 5 million pounds from the previous 50 million.
The market sharing quota period is being changed to a new basis, which will be August 1 to July 31, starting next year. This will provide the framework within which a more even milk production pattern can be achieved, which will benefit all sectors of the industry.
Our federal budget for the 1978-79 dairy program is made up as follows: $260.7 million in producer subsidy payments; $24.8 million for export assistance; $17 million in carrying charges; and $20 million for international food aid. This $20 million remains unchanged from the amount provided to the Canadian International Development Agency last year to buy skim milk powder and distribute it as part of its food aid program.
Finally, there is in that total an allowance of $6.5 million to the Canadian Dairy Commission to assist in exploring new ways to utilize skim milk powder. This amounts to a total of $329 million in federal assistance.
So far as the Canadian national requirement is concerned, this year's total has been estimated by the Canadian Milk Supply Management Committee to be 98 million hundredweights. Total market sharing quota is made up of these market requirements plus a 5 per cent sleeve. The Canadian Milk Supply Management Committee will, as it normally does, be monitoring production and demand during the year and will make any adjustments needed in quota allocation according to the policy.
I should point out that it is the responsibility of provincial boards to allocate and monitor individual quotas. It certainly is
April 13, 1978

my personal hope that provincial boards will show a special concern for the administration of their quota policies when it comes to the small producer who may have been hard hit by some of the quota cutbacks in the past. I also hope that if a quota cut is needed during the coming dairy year, then it will be made through transfer assessments or reallocation and not through direct quota cuts.
Some will be concerned because this announcement was not made prior to April 1. However, I do not believe there has ever been as much discussion and consultation between the different dairy producers concerned, provincial organizations, the market share quota committee, the management committee, and the Canadian Dairy Commission as there has been with respect to the program for this year. The last meeting of the consultative committee took place on the day the House adjourned for the Easter recess. It has taken some time to put the program together, but I know it is one of the best we have had, and I congratulate the provincial people and the marketing boards which make up the committee which worked out this program along with the Canadian Dairy Commission.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON DAIRY POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this occasion to respond on behalf of my colleagues to the minister's statement regarding the 1978-79 dairy program. I want to begin by saying that, generally speaking, the dairy year just completed has been one in which the industry has adjusted with a fairly high degree of accuracy to the policy announced a year ago.
Given the many factors which are beyond the control of our producers, they must be commended for their efforts-some at very considerable expense-and for their ability to match milk supplies with domestic consumption and that of the export market. This government ran the very serious risk a year ago, when it applied the 25-cent per hundredweight export levy on fluid milk producers, of destroying the whole national plan. That statement is not an exaggeration, and it appears that the minister today has paid a nickel's worth of attention to that particular problem.
The plan could not have been achieved without the clout of subsidy dollars. The manner in which it was put into force caused disunity among producers within their own provinces, and concern between provinces, and embedded suspicions and anger in the minds of producers and their leaders at all levels.
I am convinced that this minister and certain officials of the Canadian Dairy Commission have not recognized to this date, or choose to ignore or forget, the seriousness of their unilateral action. It is true that time is a great healer, but it is essential if this program is to continue- and it is in everyone's best interest that the program does continue-that this or any similar type of action be avoided in the future. Practically all the provinces rejected this levy, and, indeed, most of the participating provinces did not sign the agreement until well on into the last dairy year. This should provide the government with a clear indication of their dissatisfaction and their deep resentment about this type of action.
Dairy Policy
I do not know the exact situation today, but as recently as last week British Columbia had not signed the national agreement. In not doing so B.C. signified its desire to withdraw, and in accordance with the terms of the agreement B.C. is at liberty today to exercise its right to withdraw from the program. The minister said nothing about this problem today in his statement. It is important and vital to the survival of the national plan, and it must be addressed and resolved immediately.
Another issue which still remains not completely resolved is the matter of the collection of the levy based on fluid milk sales. Whatever policy is followed, it must be brought clearly into conformity with agreements reached on the obligations of the participating provinces. Changes in the sleeve portion, and indeed any changes in the plan, must be administered to eliminate any possibility that producers in any one province can gain an advantage over producers in any other province.
Maximum flexibility and autonomy should be given to each province in the management of its quota system. It is not clear from the minister's printed statement today, but the minister did indicate in his remarks that the changes in the quota year have been made from April 1, 1978, to August 1, 1979, for a 16 months' period. I believe that the intention behind such a move is to level out seasonal production. Although such a move is desirable, I doubt that any real success will be achieved in this regard without such a move being accompanied by a financial incentive.
While it is generally agreed that complete integration of fluid and industrial milk production is desirable, it must be recognized that it would not be in the best interests of the industry to have such a plan forced upon it by the federal government. But it is important that the provinces be allowed to carry out their own plans and to establish their own timetable to achieve this desirable result.
The industry people indicate that there are severe inadequacies in securing accuracy and quality of information regarding production, disappearance of products, and the movement of milk, cream, and milk products. This problem has caused serious difficulties in the past and it can and will cause difficulties in the future, if the accurately of product volumes are not more accurately identified. The Dairy Farmers' Association of Canada has made a recommendation and has called for an improved system of provincial auditing.
The government has a responsibility to ensure that when a surplus is created by certain producers who consistently overproduce, and consequently cause a general reduction in the national quota, that reduction should not be applied across the board but rather should be assessed to those producers who cause the problem and not to those who have kept within their quota. The statement today containing the new contingency level of 20 cents per 100 pounds takes this disturbing factor somewhat into consideration. In addition, in applying price increases under the federal formula, the rule of triggering price adjustments with a 4 per cent change in the formula

April 13, 1978
Dairy Policy
should be changed to 2 per cent in the interest of price stability in relation to inflationary change.
Dairy producers, and particularly the manufacturing sector, continue to call for a reduction in the level of cheese imports by 10 million to 15 million pounds. The statement today goes in the right direction, but it calls for a reduction of only five million pounds. It is interesting that only recently the minister said that import levels were not reaching that particular level. If we could find out the exact level, we would be in a position to assess intelligently whether or not this five million pounds reduction would have any benefit at all.
An import levy could be placed on imported cheese products and the revenues used to reduce the export levy or for sale and promotion of dairy products. It must be stated that every ten million pounds of cheese imports result in a loss of over $3.6 million to Canadian producers, and heavy losses to the manufacturers as well. Greater restrictions should be placed on the importation of skim milk powder and other dairy products which are imported as components. I do not have the latest figures on these amounts, but the products to which I referred have increased by some 80 per cent between 1973 and 1975.
There is no mention in the minister's statement today of the reinstatement of even a portion of the skim milk powder consumer subsidy which was recently withdrawn by the government. I spoke at some length on that issue on March 9, and I will not go into any great detail today except to say that the program should be continued in areas where no fresh milk supplies are available, in areas of high unemployment, and also in areas where the wage rates are less than the national average.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON DAIRY POLICY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON DAIRY POLICY
speechtext:
But it remains incumbent on this government to make every effort to foster and encourage a greater degree of good will and trust between government, the Canadian Dairy Commission, and the industry, than now exists. Some may scoff at that comment, but those who do give an indication that they have been out of touch with people in the dairy industry. I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that that is a major concern.
Finally, it is unfortunate, unfair to the dairy industry, and completely unacceptable to us, that policy changes continue to be announced after the effective date rather than well in advance of it. It should be noted that subsidy payments to producers have been reduced by $5.3 million, the carrying charges have been reduced by $3 million, and the $20 million commitment for food aid remains the same. There is certainly a great need to increase that $20 million for the purchase of about 60 million pounds of skim milk powder. Next time the minister consults people from the industry perhaps he would be prepared to ask them what kind of commitment they are prepared to make in that area, because I am sure they would be ready to increase their commitment from 60 million pounds to 100 million pounds of skim milk.
The minister continues to refer to this plan as being the best, to use his own favourite terminology "in the whole wide, wide
[Mr. Wise.)
world". In fact, Mr. Speaker, it is not uncommon for the minister to use the same modest description in referring to himself.
I agree that the Canadian dairy industry must be the best in the world to survive many of the programs and policies of this government. With some of the changes I have suggested today, with more consultation and co-operation and more forward planning by the government with the dairy industry, the goal referred to by the minister could be achieved.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON DAIRY POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was impressed by the last remarks made by the hon. member when he mentioned the fact that the minister always refers to "the best minister" and "the best program". I think this is one of the times when the farmers thought it would be a better program. However, this is a program which will not change very much, and in fact will not provide even the changes that were recommended by the Dairy Council of Canada at its recent convention.
The minister stated that the target for this year will be about the same as last year, that there will be a slight increase in industrial milk, but that we are still plagued with the same problems we had before. In that respect he did not mention the contribution made by individual farmers. Farmers have been plagued by two things: the actions taken by the governments, both provincial and federal, and the inability of the government and its agencies to ascertain exactly what the market will be in the forthcoming year.
Over the last four or five years the concept of establishing the dairy year has become very important to farmers and has become increasingly difficult to establish for the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan). The one thing on which I wish to congratulate him is the fact that he has only been 13 days late this year. This is an improvement on the past. The delay is caused in part by our inability to decide what the target will be and exactly where we stand in terms of quotas, because we have not done the one thing for which the dairy farmers have asked, that is, we have not been able to achieve an understanding between the marketing boards in the various provinces, the provinces, and the Canadian Dairy Commission with regard to quotas and how to operate them. As the hon. member who preceded me has said, we are unable to bring all provinces into line, with the farmer down at the bottom agreeing that this is the manner in which the program has to work and these are the contributions he will be required to make.
In drafting the press release, the minister got the best out of it. That is normal, of course. Several weeks ago I spoke with a young farmer. He is not a big farmer, nor a small farmer. He has approximately 40 heads of milk cows. At that time he indicated that his over quota levy would amount to approximately $5,600. The minister indicated that we were to receive an additional 300,000 pound quota. I think 40 cows would produce something over that. Thus, the average probably would be something over that. He indicated they would receive $2,300, and that the increase did not meet inflation. Most
April 13, 1978

farmers have not been able to make that $2,300 because they would be required to make the over quota payment. The minister is faced with a problem which most dairy farmers thought would be solved in this statement. I am referring to the recommended change in the dairy year.
One problem we have been faced with in arriving at a target quota is the movement of the dairy year to a point in time further in the year, with a period of adjustment of perhaps three or four months. Perhaps it could be from April to July. It could be a 16-month year in order to arrive at a more even quota structure. The dairy year would take into consideration part of the problem with respect to seasonal milk. The elimination of summer milk was discussed at all farm meetings. I am sure the Dairy Commission has great difficulty with this problem. Certainly it is a problem with which the industry has great difficulty. In his statement the minister did not give much consideration to that particular problem.
Like the fluid milk producers of Canada, the industrial milk producers should be required to produce milk under a monthly quota which will involve the total year, so that producers in the industrial field will not make their total production in the summer months. Total production in the summer months causes great difficulty to the cheese industry which operates year round. That particular problem has not been faced as yet.
Another problem we are faced with is skim milk powder. It would be wise to sit down sooner or later and decide whether we are going to produce any skim milk powder, whether it is worth taking off the $7 over quota levy, whether it is worth supplementing by approximately 50 cents the production of skim milk powder for international sales. Perhaps we are not receiving any advantage from the skim milk powder program. Perhaps there is a better way of handling it.
There are things which can be done in Canada to assist in levelling out surplus production. As the minister is aware, it comes from the industry as well as the producers themselves. When the average Canadian buys milk, he is not buying fluid milk from the cow. He is buying 2 per cent, skim, or some other product or by-product from the fluid field. We should put some money into the disposal of skim milk powder. It is a valuable commodity. We are attempting to give it to other countries, at the same time as indicating that it has nutritional value. Perhaps it could be distributed in Canada through a school milk program. That would cost a few dollars, but it would be better than what is occurring at the present time. Farmers are finding it easier to dump milk down the drain than putting it into the system. That is a waste of a nutritious and very useful resource. It should be distributed through a school milk program or through a food stamp program which would benefit poorer families.
Several other things should have been included in the minister's statement respecting the sales program of quotas. Last year when some farmers had huge quotas, quota was available and many people borrowed, rented or loaned quota, and it was fairly satisfactory. This year the price of quota fluctuated to an unreasonably high level. In fact, most producers have indicated that it will take two to four years of production to
Dairy Policy
pay for the industrial quota, and there is no assurance that the price will remain at that level.
There are a number of programs which could be implemented. If time permitted, I could outline a number of ways that are better to utilize skim milk powder than paying people to take it off our hands. In many cases it is delivered to countries where, if their water were added to the powder, it could become a poisonous substance. There are better ways of handling skim milk powder.
Farmers will not be very happy with the dairy program this year. It does not indicate anything of substance or any value, with the exception of the reduction of cheese imports. I am surprised and pleased with the industrial developments which have taken place in the production of cheese in Canada. Unfortunately, Kraft is one of the companies which has been involved, but companies have been able to produce probably 30 or 40 types of cheese which previously had to be imported from Europe and other parts of the world. At the present time probably 110 types, varieties or brands of cheese are being imported. With the help of the Department of Agriculture, perhaps Canada would be able to manufacture every one of those specialty cheeses.
How was the minister able to change the only thing which developed the contractual link of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) with the European Common Market? Cheese imports were reduced by another ten million pounds, but most Canadian farmers feel those imports should be stopped altogether, or a tariff should be placed on those imports in order for Canada to double its specialty cheese production.
The minister will not receive any kudos out of this year's announcement. Many things should have taken place. There should be federal leadership from the Canadian Dairy Commission to the pooling of industrial and fluid milk sales in Canada. Most farmers have made the expenditure which would allow them to produce the high quality milk which has always been available to Canadian fluid milk users. In the main, industrial milk producers are now meeting those standards. It appears to me it is time for us to give some leadership in the pooling of all milk so that it is not handled in a different manner in different provinces.
The minister has not solved the problem of over production by food-milk producers although this is something that has caused difficulty. I am sure he would not have collected from most people if we had not been paying the subsidy.
I think there are many things that can and should be done to make our dairy industry a more viable industry.
In closing, I should like to say that Canadians in general should appreciate the efforts of the dairy producers in this country. Under great hardship over the last two or three years they have been able to overcome their difficulties and establish a sound industrial and fluid milk industry which has provided milk for Canadians at a reasonable price.

April 13, 1978
Dairy Policy

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON DAIRY POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week I asked the Minister of Agriculture to announce as soon as possible the dairy policy for the current year. At that time, the minister answered proudly that he would announce it soon and that we should certainly be happy to learn that it would be the best in the world.
Now, as it looks very much like the one we had last year; it is nothing new since the quota is still 98 to 103 million hundredweights. So it is exactly the same as last year. As concerns the subsidy which remains at $2.66, I thank the minister on behalf of dairy producers, because there were rumours in my province to the effect that the federal government intended to discontinue the subsidies paid to industrial milk producers. This is further proof that the public is not always adequately informed, since I received many calls from people inquiring whether that was true or not.
Mr. Speaker, the target price per hundredweight of milk, as mentioned in the minister's statement, has been raised to $12.42, or a 24 cent increase per hundredweight. I feel, and the minister agrees with me, that this increase is far below those made in other sectors. I am convinced that at least farm and dairy producers will not be blamed for the rising inflation in Canada and the fall of the Canadian dollar.
1 am pleased, Mr. Speaker, that the import levy has been reduced to $1 per hundredweight. I wonder how it came to be set at $1, because a little further in the statement we find that "every hundredweight of in-quota industrial milk and cream will be subject to a new contingency level of 20 cents, refundable to those producers who, at year end, have managed to keep their production within national requirements."
So, it is $1 or $1.09. Who is going to decide whether it is really only $1 or $1.09? In what circumstances is this really going to be set at $1.09? Mr. Speaker, the levy on surplus cream diverted from fluid milk for industrial use, which is equivalent to 20 cents on fluid milk, is also announced in the dairy policy. This is a matter, Mr. Speaker, which gave rise last year to terrible discussions, manifestations, even confrontation here in front of parliament and this problem was solved very late in the year. I would like the minister's assurance on this question, so we could know if the management committee, the Canadian Dairy Commission and the minister really reached an agreement which will prevent manifestations of the kind we had last year.
What is less welcome, Mr. Speaker, is the raise to $7.50 of the over-quota levy and as I often said before, as have others, it is not easy for a dairy producer to control precisely the production allowed by his quota. I have been a dairy producer for some time, and I always preferred a great unit production. Our agronomists and our technicians were teaching us various formulas for improving the milk production of our cows, and with this penalty policy, as milk production is not as simple to

control as a tap, some producers must have their cows treated with injections to reduce their production, and this certainly upsets the cows. So instead of giving milk, they give "spite", because this is against the law of nature. Thus, the quality of our herds depreciates, and I am afraid that in the next few years we will have to pay for that, because it is not normal to give chemical injections for keeping the dairy cow from producing milk. Mr. Speaker, I now would like to discuss cheese imports. The minister is telling us that there will be a reduction to 45 million this year. Last year they were at 50 million.
On behalf of producers, I would like to urge the minister to stimulate research programs to make greater use of our dairy production and develop various kinds of cheese which could be made available to our Canadian consumers to eliminate the surpluses that will be penalized, according to the minister's statement. Mr. Speaker, I am convinced that the minister is sincere because he mentioned in his statement that last year small and young producers experienced problems as a result of the quotas but he also added: I also hope that if a quota cut is needed during the coming dairy year then it will be made through transfer assessments or reallocations and not through direct quota cuts.
Now if we want to ensure that a new generation will carry on in agriculture, we must not discourage the young people who run into debt and decide to buy the family land and adjoining lands to have a productive operation. Yet our laws force them to get into debt and to buy quotas to be able to. I am sure the hon. member for Levis (Mr. Guay) who is listening to me very carefully sees those things happening, because it also happens in this riding. So we should devise a formula to encourage them.
Mr. Speaker, the rise in the price of milk falls far short of the rise in production costs. It is a well known fact that electricity costs went up sharply, that gas costs went up sharply, as did the cost of farm machinery parts. On that matter, I would like to take this opportunity to ask the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) to see to it that the recommendations of the Barber Commission be implemented as soon as possible, so that farmers are not forced to pay prohibitive prices for replacement parts. Something must be done in this regard to help milk producers and improve their situation.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, to conclude I must confess that I am a little disappointed that the school year, I mean the dairy year, has not been changed. I am sorry if I said school year but I was a school commissioner for a long time and we had to talk of school years then, but what I meant was dairy year. I believe it would be an excellent solution and it should be studied further. The dairy year should be changed to run from October 1 to September 30 of the following year so that the producers would be able to eliminate from their herd the necessary number of heads for the winter months and maintain it at the established level of the quota. As everyone knows,
April 13, 1978

during the winter beef prices are higher and the dairy producers could then dispose of their cattle at prices which would bring them additional revenues. Mr. Speaker, I think that the minister should retain this proposal, and apply it to the current year as it is not too late to do so; but if they did change the dairy year, why not say so in the statement?

Mr. Speaker, I have a three-pronged question. The reason cheese is being imported is because there is a profit in it. In the past brokers have been receiving profits from its importation. I was wondering if there has been any discussion in the department to ensure that the Canadian Dairy Commission receives the profit on the importation of cheese.
With regard to the advertising program relating to cheese, will there be greater flexibility given to provinces like Alberta which has its own program? subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON DAIRY POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on the question of import/export of cheese and that profit must be there for importers/exporters to be in the business of bringing in this product, I would agree with the hon. member that we have discussed the same type of an operation which we use for butter at the present time. We need butter. On the butterfat exchange program last year we did import some butter, but that is brought in and put on the market at a domestic price. If there is any money to be made, that goes into the treasury. For instance, if butter was brought in at world price last year it would have been around 35 cents a pound, plus a little bit, I believe towards the end of the year. That was put on the domestic market at our price in Canada. The money that was made belonged to the Dairy Commission, or the Treasury of Canada, I believe you would say.
With regard to sharing of advertising, I think I know what the hon. member wants. Alberta was the only province that asked that it be given the money to advertise provincially. That decision was made by all the producers, etc., that the advertising should be national, that electronic and paper media be used. We think it has been very successful because the con-
Dairy Policy
sumption of cheese has gone up, in the case of cheddar by over 3 per cent, and specialty cheese by over 6 per cent which is a sizeable increase in any one year.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON DAIRY POLICY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, very briefly I would like to ask the minister, in view of the fact that we will now be changing the dairy year, for the first time with an additional four months for a total of 16 months, could he indicate how the quota will be determined for those four months in view of the fact those four months are in the spring and shippers generally have a higher amount of shipping during that period of time, and yet our regular shippers through the year-12 months-have a fairly steady supply of milk? How will this be determined, and will there be very close monitoring and increased monitoring by the CDC in order to make sure that whatever arrangement there is, it will not be misused by those in the shipping of milk for specific periods?

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON DAIRY POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the whole idea of changing the dairy year has come about not from the Dairy Commission solely but from the producers themselves. We want a constant production of fresh milk for those markets that are developing. Of the $6.5 million that will be used to develop new programs and new ways to sell the industrial dairy products, part at least will be going for that kind of development. We need the fresh milk for yogourt, etc. These types of products are rapidly expanding for consumption in homes and restaurants. This is an area in which we think we should be involved.
We have increased the sales of condensed milk on world markets last year by around 40 per cent. That lessens the need for butter and skim milk powder. When you can sell the complete product, condensed in a can, in some other part of the world it is better to do that even if, as the spokesman for the New Democratic Party has said, some of our fat needs must be imported, and it is better to do that because it is not so costly.
I think the monitoring system is the best we have had for a long time. The co-operation between the provinces, the provincial marketing boards, and the CDC I feel is excellent at the present time, to make sure that they know when they are getting out of line with production. I believe the hon. member for Elgin (Mr. Wise) made a comment about that when he spoke.
When one section or the other is getting out of line it is watched much closer. Under the program for this year, no longer will it be that one province over-produces and the other one pays a penalty. If a neighbour over-produces, no longer will the other neighbour pay part of that penalty. If they get out of line on the quota allowed to them, they will be the ones who will pay for it; in other words, the individual who breaks the rules. This is something which the producers want, and we want.
The four months will be reported month by month to the Dairy Commission. We know there will always be that production in that four months the hon. member is talking about. That should be taken advantage of and can be used for those products we are discussing. That is a time of year when there is an extra consumption of dairy products. Those are also some

of the better months for tourism. The advertising program will be geared to using as much of that in as many new ways as we can possibly think of.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question relates to the movement of people within Canada. If I might use the example of Alberta, in the last three years Alberta has increased its population by movement, from within Canada, by some 60,000 per year. This has placed the province of Alberta in a shortage of supply situation at times. Will the minister instruct the milk supply committee to meet again in order that we can come up with an adequate quota to reflect the movement of people in this country in order to solve the problems, particularly in Alberta and British Columbia?

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON DAIRY POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the supply management committee and the Dairy Commission are very much aware of the different areas of consumption in Canada. Even without the movement of people, certain parts of our society consume more of the product than others because of income, their way of life, and so on. It may be because of the kind of program a province may have. For example, the province of Nova Scotia has a milk program for school children. Therefore, the children there are trained, if not at home, at school, that milk is a good protein product and is highly nourishing. That has a consumption factor built in from the time they go to kindergarten. This is being tried by some of the other provincial groups. Provincial marketing boards have special advertising programs.
The Alberta producers are not in the difficult position the hon. member talked about. If he has evidence about a shortage in Alberta, it has not been brought to my attention. They had a slight surplus problem in Alberta last year. They distribute within the province, not by the federal Dairy Commission.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we are all anxious to hear the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark). However, I would first like to ask a short but important question. I hope it will elicit a brief reply. It is a simple question. The consumer subsidy on powdered skim milk has been removed. Concern has been expressed by his colleague, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet), who stated in committee the other night that it should be placed back on for certain groups. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) has also expressed concern about it. Has the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) had consultation with these two colleagues to see what can be done to offset the 40 to 50 per cent price increase on powdered skim milk which will flow from his announcement, and which will lean pretty heavily on poor people, native people, and particularly on people in the north?

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON DAIRY POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if there is a 40 or 50 per cent increase in the price of skim milk powder, something is very wrong. It should not amount to anything more than 34 cents a pound. Thirty-four on to 74 does not make a 50 per cent increase in the price of that product. Even if they add the total on to it, and there is nothing saying the store has to do it, they

will supply a quart of a healthy, life-giving substance with many of the minerals that all age groups need, for about 28 cents a quart. You cannot buy Pepsi, Coca Cola, Seven Up or any other soft drink beverage for that amount. With regard to the question of whether I am consulting with my colleagues, yes I am. I again say that I do not think that it is the position of the Department of Agriculture to be in the subsidy business. Possibly transportation should be considered. Over half the cost of food in some of the northern parts of this country is transportation. Maybe it should be in the form of more direct aid through subsidization. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I raise a question of privilege.
Earlier in the day, while commenting on the statement made by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) on the dairy policy, I made certain suggestions and I made them on the basis of a document which was delivered to me, namely the statement made by the minister to the House today and which I received just before coming to the House. So, in view of the fact that I did not have the official communique which the hon. member for Levis (Mr. Guay) handed me some time after, I therefore raise the question of privilege because I suggested a change of date in the dairy policy while the official communique contained precisely a change of date which is official.
As a result I have found myself stating things which I should have known and the fact is that it makes you look very silly when you take a position regarding a document in your hands while there actually exists another document which is more complete and more informative. I do not intend to blame
April 13, 1978

the minister for that, Mr. Speaker, but I would like to seize this opportunity so that in the future, when there is a minister's statement of such significance, we may get at least the full text of the communique while the minister himself could summarize it before us. That way, we would be in a position of total awareness regarding all the facts. I do not wish to complain needlessly, but I am convinced that my question of privilege is quite justified and well-grounded so I would appreciate if it could be taken into account.
