speakeroldname: Mr. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is appropriate that moments before I rise to speak on a budget which should have been brought in long ago, we saw introduced as a private member's bill a piece of legislation-a meat import law-which should have been introduced by a minister of the Crown, by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), some time ago. He promised three years ago he would introduce such a bill, and again he promised it would be introduced by the government this session. That responsibility was abandoned by the government and passed off to a backbencher, in the certain knowledge that, because of the way in which this government works, that piece of agricultural legislation would never see the light of day in this House.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in dealing with the budget which was brought down on Monday night by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) I have to say with real sadness that my response, as I listened to the minister deliver his first and last budget address, was very much like my reaction to the speech given by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau)-the latest in a series of televised speeches shown on CBC and CTV across the country-when he went to New York. What happened with this budget, as happened with the speech made by the Prime Minister in New York, was that the government, presented with an excellent opportunity to give Canadians some sense of economic leadership and to give the international community some certainty and confidence that there was a government here which was prepared to give economic leadership and to give some direction to our economy, failed to meet that opportunity to respond.
That opportunity was lost for two fundamental reasons. First, the government just does not want to admit how very

April 13, 1978
The Budget-Mr. Clark
serious Canada's economic problems are today. Second, this government no longer has the energy or imagination to give the Canadian economy the leadership it needs. The problems are only too well known to all of us. The Canadian dollar has fallen far below the level it should reach. The point which troubles most of us as we look at daily declines in the value of our dollar is the incompetence of this government which has created such concern among the international community. This government alone has cost us at least three points on the value of our dollar. I say "at least". It has cost this country somewhere between a billion, and one and a half billion dollars-a billion, or a billion and a half dollars wasted already because the international community-people who have to make decisions about the value and worth of the Canadian currency-just cannot find in this incompetent government anyone in whom to place their confidence.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We see the situation in this country where investment money-money which should be invested in this country to create jobs in this country, Canadian investment, and money which could come in from abroad if there were a climate in which foreign and Canadian investors could have confidence-instead of coming into this country is flooding out of it. Again, we see the rise of inflation in this country. Yesterday the figures showed it has risen once more-up to 8.8 per cent on an annual basis, an inflation rate which has been driven even higher by the finance minister's handling of the Canadian dollar.
We know the grievous situation which exists among the unemployed in Canada. More than a million Canadians are out of work now, and the government's answer to those million people is to say: It does not matter; they have unemployment insurance; they do not need to work; they can go on welfare. That is the philosophy of this government-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Shame!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: -and then they go on to say: Besides, that's not the real figure. Those are not real people, they are just women who want to work. Or: They are just young people who want to work. Mr. Speaker, that is a shameful attitude.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: A heartless minister.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Of course women in this country want to work. And they have the right to expect that this will be a modern community in which they can find work to do, if that is what they want. Of course young people in this country want to work. And they want to be able to start their careers with jobs to go to, rather than having to go to the Unemployment Insurance Commission. They should want to work. But in too many cases, among women and among young people, it is not simply a matter of wanting to work; it is a matter of having to work.
If the Minister of Finance, who so cavalierly blames unemployment on the women of Canada, would take a look at the actual situation of many of the women who are working, he would know that in many cases they are working because they have to work. He would know that if they did not work, or if they were not seeking work, their families would be without bread on the table, their children would be without the kind of future which should be theirs in a country such as Canada. These women have to work because we have a government which has let costs get out of control and which has destroyed the sense of possibility which used to be the basis of the Canadian nation.
The Prime Minister, with that lack of concern for economic matters and for the situation of the ordinary Canadian which he has demonstrated over the years, blames these problems on the world. He says they result from world conditions. It used to be the weather that he blamed, but now he needs a different explanation. The real problem is the ten-year failure of this government. Of course the world is tough. The Prime Minister should have known this from all his reading and all his travels. We live in a tough, hard world, but no matter how tough it is, ours is a country which should lead the world and not fall helplessly behind as we have under the direction and policies of this government-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The difficulty is that the government is just worn out. Even when it was a young government-if you can cast your mind back that far to a point at which this government had some energy-when its best ministers were coming in instead of going out, and I refer to those like the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) who is across the aisle, back when it had energy and imagination, this government even then laid the basis for many of our economic problems of today by putting its priorities in areas other than the Canadian economy. It is uncontestable that by focusing so much exclusive attention on language policy and on theories like the contractual link, the government ignored the realities of the Canadian economy. Not only did it set the stage for the economic problems we now have, but it also sowed fresh seeds of separatism in the province of Quebec. That is the legacy of this government.
When it is forced to face the economic reality of Canada, this government is just too worn out to take command. Government members content themselves with trying to fool people instead of trying to lead them. There has been an absolute failure in economic leadership. I ask the House to consider these facts.
Tomorrow, April 14, is the date for the termination of controls, and two points are important for the House and the country to recognize. This government broke its word when it brought in controls. That is well known, but the government also broke its word in the way it operated the controls. Hon. members and the people of Canada will recall that when the Prime Minister introduced controls, he went out and promised
[Mr. Clark.}
April 13, 1978

that there would be major reforms in housing policy, in energy policy, and in other areas where change was needed, and that we would use the period of controls and the atmosphere of emergency to achieve those changes. Well, none of those reforms has come about. Untold millions in Canadian investment left this country because of the uncertainty that was generated by the controls regime, and inflation today, which was "wrestled to the ground" and which this government said it would end, stands at 8.8 per cent, and is rising.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: A shameful record.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In October the new minister took a half step toward dealing with this problem when he brought down a budget which was not a budget. It was a document marked by a stimulus which was not a stimulus. The centrepiece of that proposal, as hon. members will recall, was a two-month tax cut of about $700 million, and the evidence is that it had almost no impact on the Canadian economy because the initiative of the government in October was too timid and far too limited. We asked for a real budget to be brought forward, and this government ducked, delayed, refused, sought every refuge and subterfuge it could, and finally brought in a patch-up budget which has the same weaknesses as the last excuse for stimulus. There is no over-all economic framework in this budget. There is no commitment to cut government spending, and no stimulus permanent enough to make a real difference in creating jobs and growth for Canadians.

Of course the budget features one or two provisions which we can support; there has never been any budget which did not contain valid proposals. I am pleased to note that the minister has complied with our request for action to promote research and development and has at least restored the tax deduction for research and development set under the Diefenbaker administration, a deduction which was subsequently removed by the Liberals. We are also pleased to note that our suggestion for a more equitable treatment of incorporated family farms has been accepted. We were also satisfied with the necessary options suggested for the pension plan as well as the limited incentives granted in the transportation and energy areas.

The Minister of Finance faced three major challenges in preparing this budget, but the sad report card is that he failed on each challenge. The most immediate challenge was to create jobs for Canadians. More than one million Canadians are out of work, and the challenge was to create jobs by stimulating the economy. By the government's own calculations, the stimulus the minister proposed will create just a few more jobs in six months than the government lost last month alone because of its economic policies.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Shame!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The second challenge was to halt the costly run on the Canadian dollar. Well, the results are in. Every half
The Budget-Mr. Clark
measure this minister takes drives the dollar further down. Just an hour after the minister finished reading his budget statement, the vice-president of the Bank of America said on CBC television from New York that nothing in the budget would help bolster the dollar or help assure international investors about the long-term prospects of the Canadian economy. In this morning's Montreal Gazette a senior trader was quoted as saying:
The events of the last few days have only increased downward pressure on the dollar. First came what was seen as a neutral budget, then poor unemployment figures and (then) figures showing a sharp rise in the consumer price index.
Every action this government takes makes our dollar figures worse, and one of the reasons is that this government will not come clean with the Canadian people, spell out its strategy, and take full measures instead of half measures. The government knows it must do that.
The third and perhaps most important challenge the minister faced was to restore some sense of confidence in Canadians and to demonstrate that we have here a national government which is doing more than plugging the leaks in a sinking ship. The centrepiece of this budget reflects the minister's view of Canada's future. That reflection of his view causes alarm among many Canadians because he thinks of our future in terms of six months, and he brings in a stimulus which will stop after six months. It will stop when it is needed most, when unemployment grows most acute in this country.
That measure may be considered to be politically clever. That measure provides election stimulus-or so the minister hopes-if not economic stimulus, and it perpetuates the old pattern of this government of creating problems for the provinces. We can be sure that particularly in the next two or three months the federal government will be going around this country and taking credit for introducing this measure. However, the provinces will bear the burden of restoring this tax, and that will be a particularly heavy burden because the provinces will be seen to be increasing sales taxes when this half measure ends. That will happen at precisely the time when unemployment in Canada becomes most acute. One wonders how Premier Regan of Nova Scotia will welcome that particular burden from his Liberal friends in Ottawa.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He won't be there.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: As my colleague from Nova Scotia reminds me, Premier Regan, who represents the western beachhead of Liberal strength in this country, will probably not be there come fall. If he is, and if he goes to the people and has to defend the re-introduction of sales taxes because of the shortsighted economic policies of his colleagues in Ottawa, he will certainly be on his way down the road after an election in his province.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Then he will know how Bourassa felt.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
With an aptness which Canadians who are concerned about the national unity debate should clearly understand, my colleague says that Premier Regan will know how Premier Bourassa felt, because Premier Bourassa was

April 13, 1978
The Budget-Mr. Clark
betrayed in every step and in every initiative he took by people in his own party.
The Minister of Finance could have met the challenges which were before him. He owed it to Canada at least to try to meet them. He could have produced the major permanent economic stimulus which is needed to create jobs in this country. He could have learned from his own experience of last October that half measures just will not work. They did not work in October; why does he think they will work now? We told him then that a two-month tax cut would not turn the economy around, and I tell him now that a six-month tax cut will not do so either.
Granted, there might be some small economic bump this summer. That might help the Liberals just a little bit during the only period in which they are interested, the period of the election campaign. I hope that we do get that economic bump, I hope there is some effect. But, sir, I repeat this because it is the fundamental weakness, not only in this legislation, but in the thinking of this short-term, part-time government. The impact of this measure stops when it is needed most. We have a stimulus that stops when a stimulus is most needed. We have a job creation measure that stops in October and November when the need for jobs in this winter country is at its most acute.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The minister says he cannot afford a larger stimulus. He said the government cannot find another nickel to cut. They could not find it in AECL, they could not find it in "Air Otto"-I see the flying minister has temporarily left the House-they could not find it in the advertising programs that the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) told the House yesterday he intends to bring in to encourage buying in Canada. Get this, the Government of Canada intends to run advertising programs to persuade the Government of Canada to buy in Canada!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is the only way he can reach his colleagues.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It may well be that the impact of this budget upon the native province of the temporary member for Crowfoot indicates that the only way he can reach his colleagues and influence their deliberations is by advertising.
I say to the minister that I could find some saving in AECL, and I could find some savings in the advertising programs of the government, as well as in the extravagant travels of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) and in a number of other areas which I spelled out for the minister before, and which I will spell out again later in this debate. I could find some savings also in the fact that if we get more Canadians to work in this country, we will get them off the unemployment insurance rolls.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I just cannot conceive of how a modern government which dares to call itself liberal, which dares to follow its tradition of building in this country, would prefer to spend on unemployment insurance rather than to spend on jobs, this from the party of C. D. Howe, from the party of people who have encouraged Canadians in the past to go out to build and to work. The tradition of the builders in the Liberal party has been put in the ground and buried by that party which prefers to encourage Canadians to go on welfare rather than to go to work.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We need a tax cut of at least $2 billion now. It should be a permanent tax cut, not some kind of six months' wonder. It should be a tax cut which gives Canadians back some of their money rather than just lending it to them for 180 days.
We propose just such a permanent measure, putting money permanently in the hands of lower and middle income Canadians, people who are most likely to spend that money quickly, to spend it in Canada, to spend it on Canadian goods, and by spending to allow Canadian plants and industries, which are now operating under capacity, to produce more goods and to go out and hire some of that army of Canadian unemployed. That is what we need to create jobs in this country now.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Among other advantages, that proposal is guided by an elemental sense of social justice. The Trudeau government offers the rich the same kind of stimulus as it offers the poor. Indeed, in many ways this minister offers the rich more. Under its proposal, the cost of Cadillacs will go down but the price of food will remain the same.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Shame!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That shows the priorities of this government. Among other dangers, the failure to bring in a budget which would be a document of economic leadership has added to the great sense of uncertainty about our future in this country. That is not the first time, because if this government is expert in anything, it is expert in uncertainty.
[ Translation]
One of the basic causes of the problems which occurred during the Trudeau years was the government's refusal to consider the provinces, business and labour as true partners in our society. It refused to consult the unions before deciding on the Economic Council of Canada for the post control period and it refused to clearly state the regulations which would allow oil companies to expand their exploration in the north. It refused to divulge to the provinces the outline of its national policy, which would have given the provinces a basis on which to develop their own plans of action. It even refused to publish the new Bank Act. We know, Mr. Speaker, that the new act is drafted and ready, but the Trudeau government continues to hide it. Why? That is true and the minister knows it is.
April 13, 1978

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It has not yet been translated into French.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is available. The minister can answer questions asked in the House on the policy, on different aspects of that piece of legislation. I asked a question regarding the directions. I asked the minister to tell Canadians, here in Parliament and throughout the country, if the government intends to include caisses populaires and credit unions in that legislation. He refused to answer. He replied that we had to wait and study the legislation. The first time he said it was not for the House of Commons. Now, his excuse is that it is not translated. This is a matter which involves the government's policy and we are wondering whether the Trudeau government intends to include the Quebec caisses populaires and the credit unions in the Bank Act.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What are your views about it?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My policy, as leader of the opposition, is to force the government into putting an end to the practice of hiding the truth from Canadians and, when it has a policy or a bill it must say so here in the House of Commons. I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that the bill is hidden somewhere, not because of the translation, but because the government intends to act against the interest of the Quebec people and caisses populaires. They want to keep their intentions quiet until the election. The impact will be serious on the province of Quebec, and it is irresponsible on the part of the Trudeau government to hide the truth about its intentions from Quebecers.
The minister wants to speak now. Perhaps later, since he is in the frame of mind to speak now, he could indicate exactly what the government intends to do about the Quebec caisses populaires. The bill is ready, he said so today, the policy is very clear on the matter. Why then should the policy be kept locked up, why does the minister refuse now to tell the House of Commons, Parliament, the Quebec people, the truth about the policy of the government? Why hide it? That is the question I now put to the government.
It must be remembered that it was that same Trudeau government that condemned the controls program, and then adopted one. Clearly, the Trudeau government cannot be trusted. Today the government must reveal its intentions with regard to the caisses populaires. They are threatened now by the government; the government should at least put out the bill: it is ready and only awaiting translation. It cannot be kept hidden any longer and serve to betray the Canadian people as it was betrayed in the case of the controls program.
This budget and this budget debate demonstrate the fundamental difference between the Liberal party and the Progressive Conservative party, in our view of the country, in our view of the economy, and in our view of the purpose of the budget.
The Budget-Mr. Clark
They regard the budget as a place to bluff. We regard the budget as a place to build.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Instead of a temporary tax cut which stops when unemployment becomes acute, we would have introduced a permanent tax cut which would have created jobs into the foreseeable future. Instead of ignoring Canadian small business, which is the backbone of the Canadian enterprise system, we would have introduced a tax credit to a limit of $5,000 per year to encourage Canadians to invest in Canadian small business.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Instead of six months' help in the summertime in Atlantic Canada, we would have combined the permanent stimulus of a permanent tax cut with the introduction of long term tax contracts to draw strong industry to build and to stay in Quebec and in Atlantic Canada.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Most important, instead of a budget which takes such a limited view of Canada, which sees Canada as a six months' place, we would have used this budget to start the process of building a national development policy for Canada.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
This budget fails completely to give Canadians any sense of national direction. In that respect, I regret to say it is a budget very much in the Trudeau tradition. We have had a full decade of such budgets, budgets which tinker with the tax rates but offer no framework, no direction, no development plan on which Canadians can count and in which they can lay their own plans and set their own priorities. There is no excuse for any of that full decade of drift, this full decade of opportunities lost for Canada.
This minister has even less excuse, because at the first ministers' conference in February, the provinces of Canada, which take their responsibility by and large much more seriously than this government does, gave the government a lengthy list of positive, constructive proposals which could form part of a new national development strategy. Thanks to the premiers, the minister had plenty of raw material from which to draw. Yet this budget does not implement and does not even deal with a single one of those proposals. It merely confirms that, having succeeded in getting the government a few hours of television time, the first ministers' conference is as dead as a dodo. In terms of a policy instrument, it has been a deliberate waste of the time of the premiers of Canada.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Had this budget been ours, it would have spelled out a comprehensive plan for national development, not for a few months but for at least the next five years. As well as permanent stimulus, it would have spelled out the means we

April 13, 1978
The Budget-Mr. Clark
would take as the government to reduce significantly government's demands on the productive sectors of our society. I have presented this proposal to the government before. It is a proposal including sunset laws, which this nation very urgently needs. It is a proposal involving new means of budgetary control; a proposal involving deregulation; and a proposal requiring a tough-minded review of Crown corporations by this government which has more Crown corporations than it can count.
The Prime Minister talked about it being a tough world. Well, it is a tough world. He should stop just talking about that and begin to develop policies which recognize that we have to compete, grow, and build in a tough world. It is clear that the basis of any national development plan that we have to bring in, and certainly the basis of the plan we intend to bring in when we form the government, would be to build upon the great natural strengths of this country, build upon those strengths where we can become competitive in the world. Not just competitive, we should build upon those strengths where we can become leaders in the world. That used to be a concept of Liberal governments. There was a lot wrong with C. D. Howe, as the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) will remember. There was a lot wrong, but he was a man who believed in making Canada a leader in the world. That used to be a tradition of the Liberal party. It is no longer. That tradition has gone from the Liberal party and it sits now in the Conservative party.
Some hon. Members; Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Who is C. D. Howe?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The minister indicates not only has he forgotten the traditions of C. D. Howe, he does not even know who the man was.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I suppose we cannot expect much more vision backward than we find forward from a minister of the Crown who brings in an economic policy for only six months.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Does he remember Laurier?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I hope he remembers Laurier. Laurier was the prime minister who said that the twentieth century can belong to Canada. The Progressive Conservative party is the only party in Canada today which can begin to realize the promise of making the twentieth century ours.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I should like to enumerate some of the natural strengths upon which we can build as a country. For example, Canada already is one of the world's major producers of food. We can build on that strength by increasing our investment in food products and processes; by developing the storage vessels and processing capacity which our fishermen need to get the most out of the 200-mile limit; by aggressively seeking markets
[Mr. Clark.)
for our dairy products in places like Britain where cheddar cheese is actually being rationed today. We would stop talking about the OPEC crisis of the past. We would start acting on Canada's energy potential for the future by accelerating development of tar sands and heavy oil deposits, by getting on with tidal power.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Look at the budget.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am pleased to hear from the hon. Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie). He is the minister who is left at home when Canada goes abroad to negotiate treaties in his domain.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: As I indicated, we would do that by getting on with tidal power and by moving forward on the construction of a reversible pipeline to Atlantic Canada. We would acknowledge the success of a company in this country like Northern Telecom, in becoming a major exporter of communications equipment. We would build on the strength of that industry, especially its expertise in long distance and remote area communications. We would use the billions of dollars Canada is going to have to invest in fishing, defence and energy vessels. It would be used as the base for a world scale shipbuilding industry in Atlantic Canada.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: As the premier of Ontario has proposed, we would use our domestic need to improve rail services in the Windsor-Quebec corridor to assist our transportation industry to meet competitive world standards. We would end the atrocious situation at the port of Vancouver where, on average, 24 vessels are always waiting two to six weeks to load Canadian grain.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Right on!

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: At the expense of farmers.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We would recognize in our national development policy the fact that in the Middle East alone countries are planning to invest more than $200 billion over the next decade in infrastructure-in schools, in communications, in transportation and in housing. In this country we have companies like ATCO which have succeeded in this kind of world market despite the obstacles governments have put in their way. We would get behind more Canadian companies that have the experience and expertise to serve these markets.
The budget refers to research and development. By our debate in parliament some weeks ago, we forced the government to stop ignoring innovation in this country. But it is ironic to note what they count as an accomplishment. They have reinstated precisely the policy that a Progressive Conservative government introduced in 1961-the government of my colleague, the right hon. member for Prince Albert. A
April 13, 1978

Liberal government abandoned that policy as quickly as it could. We are glad to have it back; but bringing back the status quo in research and development is not enough.
One of the fundamental failures of this government has been the failure to recognize how important it is for Canada's research and development policy to become the basis of our ability to grow in the world. We have a serious problem-more serious, probably, than that faced by any other industrialized nation-in that so much of our natural research capacity is drained out of Canada to head offices elsewhere. That means that the specific intent of much of Canada's innovation policy must be to encourage Canadian scientists to stay at home and to encourage Canadian companies to build on Canadian strengths in a world that needs our innovation. The government has opened the door it closed several years ago. But there is no sense of direction to their innovation policy-just as there is no sense of direction to their economic policy.
That is the tragedy here. We have a nation of people who want to go to work-of provinces who want to cooperate as partners in economic growth-and of plants that are operating well below capacity. We are a nation that was once respected in the world, that was once a source of pride at home. Now we are a country whose Prime Minister tells its young to leave.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Shame!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: This is a government which, in a decade, has debased our currency, divided our country and destroyed the natural confidence of Canadians in this country. They had an opportunity, in this budget, to begin to turn that around. But they are too old, too worn out, and once again they show themselves blind to the possibilities of this country.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to say at the outset that I thoroughly enjoyed the speech made by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark). I felt it could have effectively been divided into two parts. The first part, and I think the most interesting in many respects, was the proposals he made to indicate how he would have cut taxes in the budget and how he would have cut services in the government. I think that is an appropriate position for a Tory leader.
The second half of his speech, however, was devoted not only to spending all the money he was going to cut but to spending that and more. It seems to me that the Leader of the Opposition is trying to have it two ways. He is trying to say that on the one hand he would cut taxes, cut services, and have a lean and hungry government, and that, on the other hand, there are a great many things they would want to do and a great many things that have to be done, and they are not only prepared to spend the $2 billion or whatever amount they are going to cut, but even more.
It seems to me the speech of the Leader of the Opposition would have been far more effective had it concentrated on one of those two themes, instead of trying to combine the two,
The Budget-Mr. Reid
which just will not wash. If I could give the Leader of the Opposition any advice, I would suggest that he pay some attention to the two themes he was discussing and choose one or the other, but not choose both, because that will make the next election much too easy for the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien).
The Leader of the Opposition took the opportunity to quote some comments favourable to his side. I think it is only fair to indicate that there is a division of opinion in terms of the situation with the budget. Let me quote from this morning's Globe and Mail some remarks made by the chief economist of the Bank of Montreal. An article on the first page of the Business Section reports him as follows;
'It follows that in my view there is no basic justification for the Canadian dollar to continue to slide, and before long, one could expect to see some improvement,
' Jack Toten told a seminar on Canada in the world economy.
The article goes on to say:
The lower Canadian dollar, causing higher prices for necessary imports, does increase inflation in Canada, he said. 'Quite obviously, if we fail to hold down increases in wages and costs to something like those experienced in the United States, our position will once again deteriorate and the dollar will inevitably decline.'
He pointed out that jobs would be created in Canada as a result of the decline of the dollar, because our costs are too high. There is no indication by industry or labour that they would voluntarily lower those costs, so the market is doing it for us. I think we have to admit on balance that if we cannot sell what we are producing at high wages, we are better to produce what we can at a cost which is more reasonable in the world economy. That will put people back to work and get our dollar back to where it belongs and ensure that jobs are created.
In the same newspaper the columnist Ronald Anderson had some comments to make about the way the budget was perceived by the business sector of Canada. He said:
Reaction to the budget indicated that the private sector, by and large, regards it as an acceptable and responsible budget. It is questionable whether it would have been so regarded if the sales tax program had been more ambitious, with a federal cost of, say, $1.5 billion. Furthermore, provinces that are prepared to cooperate in a six-month program may not have agreed to a one-year reduction.
That seems to me to be eminent good sense. I think the Leader of the Opposition hit on a good point by accident when he commented that if you want to stimulate the economy by spending, you help people at the lower end of the income scale. I think the point is made explicit in the subamendment presented by the New Democratic Party. There is an argument to be made about how best to stimulate spending at the lower end of the income scale, however.
It is obvious to anyone who has looked at economics that the most regressive tax is a sales tax levied by the federal government, and more particularly a retail sales tax levied by a provincial government. I think we understand why those taxes are there, but if you were trying to stimulate the economy it seems to me the fastest, most expeditious, and easiest way to do it would be through the reduction of sales tax.
The important thing-and it is difficult for hon. members opposite to acknowledge it-is that this was done with cooper-

April 13, 1978
The Budget-Mr. Reid
ation from provincial governments. It was a joint economic effort, not an initiative of the federal government alone. It followed upon what was decided at the premiers' conference instead of what the Leader of the Opposition says, that it was initiated by the Minister of Finance. Let us give credit where it is due-to the provincial premiers and the provincial ministers of finance as well. It means that in Canada we have entered into a new era of trying to determine federal and provincial priorities together. This is a unique achievement, it is the first time, to my knowledge, that it has happened.
We should go further and point out to members opposite that this follows up the agreements which were reached when the House of Commons passed the federal arrangements bill that took a fair chunk of federal spending. This was turned over to the provinces without strings, and is surely a tremendous initiative in federal-provincial relations. I should also point out it is a substantial area of federal budgetary funds over which the Minister of Finance now has no control and is not able to direct.
I want to take a look now at some of the proposals which the Leader of the Opposition has produced in terms of cutting spending. The question of the dollar is a question in many respects of confidence, of how sound our economy is and how sound our policies are. Let us be frank; we have a problem in Canada in that the federal government has a policy and we have ten provincial premiers who may have different policies. Often it is difficult to coordinate these policies.
As Premier Davis said at the first ministers' meeting, it is very difficult for an investor to understand that he must deal with ten separate industrial policies. I think Premier Davis is right to point out that an industrial policy is not necessarily within the purview of the federal government but rather is within the purview of the provincial government.
What would happen if we had the policies as enunciated by the Leader of the Opposition and the official critic of the opposition? It seems to me that the first effect it would have would make the dollar even more unstable than it is now-

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is impossible.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Why do I say that? I say it because the calculations which I have before me indicate that the programs of tax cuts and other tax measures which they have just suggested would appear-and I use the word "appear" because nobody can get a grip on them since they have been so unspecific-to cost in the range of $2.5 billion to $3 billion. They would seek to offset a part of this through a reduction in government spending.
I am sure it would be possible for a Conservative government, if it ever formed that at the federal level, to follow the example of Premier Lyon in Manitoba who has shown the way to destruction of social services by putting the burden of inflation on the backs of the poor. In Manitoba, I am told, if they do not have a display of at least 2,000 people on a regular day that it is a boring day in the Manitoba legislature. Those

members on the Conservative side should ask the hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Smith) just what the cuts have meant to his constituency and ask what it means for his chances of re-election.
It seems to me the deficit that is envisaged by the Conservative party would be enough to send the dollar scurrying down faster than anyone could anticipate. Let me give you three responses to this. First of all, the Canadian dollar exchange rate could drop sharply, leading to an accelerated rate of inflation through the price of imports. This would cause financial markets to view such an increase in the deficit as constituting irresponsible action. I emphasize the word irresponsible. The point is, as I quoted Mr. Anderson from the Globe and Mail earlier, that the business community, the private market, consider that the cuts which were made by the Minister of Finance to be appropriate under the circumstances. They further consider that the means taken to get that money quickly into circulation was appropriate, and done in as speedy a way as could be devised.
Secondly, if the money supply was not increased, and we are not clear at the moment just what the status of the official opposition is on this, the larger deficit would force interest rates up higher, hurting all private borrowers and increasing the cost of maintaining the public deficit now.
It seems that some of us were disappointed in the speech made by the Leader of the Opposition. From the build-up he received we anticipated he would come in as a knight on a white charger and be able to produce the necessary miracles from his hip pocket. We found no miracles, unfortunately. We did find a rather interesting stump speech which he was trying out on the House of Commons. He made a number of charges which I feel are totally irresponsible and not valid.
One of these charges deals with the question of the unemployment figures for women and young people. I am sure we all agree without question that this is indeed a very serious matter. In the comment which the Leader of the Opposition made in speaking of the high unemployment rate we have in Canada, he made a remarkable omission. He did not admit that from March last year to March this year some 305,000 new jobs have been created in Canada. This is a remarkable achievement for an economy which we all agree is not performing as well as we would like. I would go further and point out that that increase in the number of new jobs created in Canada is the third highest in the last 15 years. That surely is a remarkable record, Mr. Speaker.
If one wishes to discuss the economy and the budgetary problems, one has to put these things in proportion. Canada is in a unique position. A baby boom occurred in Canada. Those of us who pay attention to what is going on in local communities know that the result of that baby boom has moved now through the elementary system causing schools to be closed and along with that teachers are finding it difficult to get jobs. This lack of people coming into the school system is now beginning to affect the high schools, and the universities are planning for it. It is a remarkable phenomenon which is unique to Canada. So in the 1960's and 1970's the Government of
April 13, 1978

Canada threw the economy wide open to make sure there were as many jobs as possible available for these people coming into the work force. That tends to be the same principle we have in effect today.
It is also important to note, Mr. Speaker, that Canada has one of the highest participation rates in the work force by women and young people. That is a fact. If to admit these facts is an attack on youth and women in the work force, then I suppose anybody who looks at the facts is guilty of pointing out these embarrassing things.
It is important to recognize what is going on and, on the basis of those facts, to look for solutions. Let me take a look at the situation in terms of the labour force.
Canada's unemployment problem should be looked at in the context of the baby boom and the young people coming into the work force, and in the context of this not happening in the world economy as a whole. If we look at the Canadian record of youth employment from 1971 to 1976 we find that employment increased more rapidly in that period of time in Canada than in almost any other country in the world; three per cent per year on average in Canada; two per cent per year on average in the United States, and less than 1 per cent for the countries of Europe, and Japan. It is surely a remarkable record, Mr. Speaker. This is a record which the Tories would be well to recognize when they make their speeches.
Youth unemployment is a phenomenon which is not unique to Canada. The severity in Canada, however, is less than it is in the United States, less than it is in Italy, less than it is in France. It is the same as it is in the United Kingdom, and it is worse than it is in Japan and Germany. Not a bad record. If you measure this as a ratio of youth to adults unemployed you come up with a figure in 1977 of 2.5 in Canada and three in the United States. Certainly a creditable performance indeed. I would like to point out also that in terms of youth unemployment the money which the government is putting into Young Canada Works this summer amounts to direct job creation.
We all agree that jobs in the private sector, permanent, steady, well paying jobs, are the ideal. However, if you want to deal with an economic problem you cannot pull levers today that are going to have an effect further down the line in a year or two. It is often said that by the time you pull one of the major economic levers, what you get is a result within a year or 18 months. The problem is more urgent.
The government has moved smartly and quickly into the field of direct job creation. The programs we have initiated in Canada, and I stress the word initiated, are now being copied throughout the world. We have been innovators in dealing with direct job creation. That should be acknowledged by the opposition parties. I believe it would make their job much more honest and easy.
There have been tremendous gains in real income in Canada. Real personal income per capita in 1971 was $3,426. In 1977, and I am using a constant 1971 dollar, that had risen to $4,650. That means, after accounting for inflation, personal
The Budget-Mr. Reid
incomes rose by $1,224. That is a very impressive performance in anyone's income.
We always forget the international context. In the speech today by the Leader of the Opposition, he did his best to denigrate any external influence. He said it is a tough world out there, but basically we can solve all our problems domestically. If he takes that attitude, he does himself a disservice.
The Leader of the Opposition should cast his mind back to what was the turning point in modern world economic history, August 15, 1971, the day President Nixon took the world off the gold standard, the day he imposed wage and price controls in the United States. That basically was the day which signalled the breakdown of the Bretton Woods economic system that was constructed so laboriously after World War II.
We have not yet got a truly functioning, operating international economy. We have a system that has been patched together. Canada, as one of the countries so heavily dependent on foreign trade and the international exchange markets of the world, has suffered the most from this change.
If we do not take these changes into account, we really do not understand what happens. Canada, above all nations, is dependent upon world trade. We certainly cannot expect our economy to grow any faster than those of our competitors.
The Leader of the Opposition would have been wise indeed to have read the transcript of the President's address on inflation that was given yesterday. The President of the United States pointed out he was losing some $45 billion a year on oil imports. That means $45 billion in purchasing power is leaving the United States.
Our figure, now that we have become a net importer of oil, is about $2 billion a year. That money goes basically to the Middle East. Even more important, it is going into the hands of people who have no background in spending. By and large, there is a great gap between that money going out and being recycled.
The kind of money you could look forward to in past years to taking and recycling through our economy is no longer available to us in those amounts. This massive transfer of wealth is unparalleled in modern history. It has gone from the North American continent, the Common Market nations and Japan, what we call the western industrialized nations, to the Middle East, an area of tremendous political instability. That does not make anybody sleep well at night. It is an important factor we have to remember.
Who can remember the time in 1972-74 when there was tremendous world demand for North American food supplies, and when the growers of Australia, New Zealand and Argentina were virtually wiped out? In 1974 nobody protested the rise in food prices. We were all worried where the next supply would come from. Who can forget the droughts suffered in the western part of the United States and the western part of Canada?
Let me take it a step further. One of the most unique things that happened in the economic front in those days was the fact that for the first time the economies of all of the western world

April 13, 1978
The Budget-Mr. Reid
came together in synchronization. Normally the situation was that there were some strong economies going up and some going down. Now we are all in synchronization. In 1972 to 1975, we went up together, a single boom. We have gone down together since. We are all in recession together, and we are all fighting to get out. The amount of international cooperation which is required at the present time is not forthcoming.
I want to refer hon. members to an interesting article in the March 18, 1978, edition of the Toronto Star by Anthony Westell. He refers to an interesting speech made by a Labour member of parliament in Great Britain. He indicates that one of the problems facing the western economies is the question of moving the surpluses and deficits around. He makes the point that countries like Germany and Japan are desperate to create substantial surpluses in their trading accounts in order to have the funds necessary to buy the oil which they require to keep their economies going. What they are doing is deliberately, from self interest, and who can blame them, moving in this way. What it means to us and to North America is that this mad scramble for surpluses is forcing recession in a number of countries, particularly the United States which has the most grievous outflow of all. Let me quote from his column:
In short, in the scramble to earn enough in trade to pay for oil, developed countries are forcing each other into recession. They ought to realize what is happening and stop before it is too late.
He then quotes Mr. Lever:
'The surplus countries must not seek to impose, and the deficit countries must not accept, mutually injurious deflation with currency wars and lengthening dole queues.'
That is the fact of the matter. It is an analysis that makes some sense and indicates some of the substantial nature of the problems we face.
When I take you back into this little history lesson, I then come to the formation and effective action of the OPEC oil cartel. The increases in North America, the price we had to pay for imported oil on which we were all dependent, were massive. If western society has an Achilles heel anywhere, it is the way we use energy. Energy is North American society's Achilles heel.
Since World War II, our whole economy has been based in terms of cheap and abundant energy. Now we find that oil is no longer cheap, nor is it abundant. Two of the major terms on which we have based our economy have been demolished in one blow.
Perhaps it should be pointed out that the Arabs and the OPEC nations did us a favour. To some extent Canada and North American society at that time were living in a fool's paradise, thinking this could go on forever. Now we know it is not possible, that changes have to be made.
North American society, and Canada in particular, will have to go through a massive change. No longer can we base our economy on cheap and abundant oil. We have to re-examine the roots of this social and industrial policy, based on these two fundamental concepts. This is serious business indeed.

I would have thought the Leader of the Opposition would have dug a little deeper into what is going on and explained his view on these matters to the House. He cannot cavalierly dismiss them as being outside his purview or outside his concern.
The Leader of the Opposition had an opportunity to develop some interesting points and engage in a debate of some substance. He did not. He deliberately chose not to do that. I can certainly understand why. It would have forced him to change his views on a number of the points that he made.
I read with a great deal of interest the speech made by the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge (Mr. Saltsman), who always makes an interesting speech in the House of Commons. At this point I should indicate that I am one of those who are sorry to see the hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Gillies) make the decision to retire. I can certainly understand the pressures he went through, and the reasons. He is another gentleman who has always had something interesting and of substance to say. I must say that in economic matters it is difficult to get substance in this House.
Let me deal with the point which was made very well indeed by the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge, namely, that the minister's forecasts were all wrong. I agree. I think there is no one who would agree more with that proposition than the Minister of Finance himself. If you take a look at the forecasting institutions in Canada you will find that in the sixties, by and large, their figures were accurate and could be relied upon. But if you look at the seventies, you will find that nobody's forecasting figures are worth the paper they are printed on.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: But nobody is as wrong as the minister.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
But the point I am trying to make is that the traditions and experience built up in the sixties which allowed the government, by and large, to run the economy reasonably well and to provide a remarkable number of jobs for the tremendous number of people entering the labour force, have all been wiped out by the changes which took place and which I have described, starting on August 15, 1971.
The old techniques no longer work. And if anyone doubts this let them take any of the major economic houses, and they will find that, by and large, the accuracy rate has dropped off substantially. What this means is policy makers are increasingly in the dark as to what is going to happen.
A perfect example is what happened to the mini-budget of last fall. Certain things were expected to take place as a result of the tax cut. It was expected that additional money would go into the consumer spending side of things. What do we find? According to the figures which are coming out, we find that very little of that money went into the consumer spending side. Where did it go? I think it went into savings. I think the bulk of it went into savings. So it strikes me that when you find personal tax cuts going into the savings side instead of into the spending side, although the concept is, in my judgment, virt-
April 13, 1978

uous for private persons but almost disastrous for society as we have constructed it, it makes no sense for the Minister of Finance to contemplate personal tax cuts at all. It makes no sense, either, in this economy for any party to advocate them.
It does make sense, though, to attack the retail sales taxes because this can exercise a direct and immediate effect not only in terms of consumption but in terms of the inflation rate. We do require these cuts in sales tax at the retail level in order to cut down the inflation rate caused by the devaluation of the Canadian dollar. One will balance the other.
I think the budget met a number of disparate points remarkably well and that both the minister and the provincial premiers deserve a great deal of credit for the action they took.
I want to deal with one last point. The last point I want to deal with is the question of where do we go, how do we go, from here.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Go Conservative!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It seems to me we have to look at a number of things which are rather foreign to the way in which Canadian governments, and I include the provinces, have approached the business of stimulating the economy. I have given the example of personal income tax cuts and its relative uselessness in current circumstances.
Take another favourite fiscal tool which was used with great success during the sixties. I refer to the corporation tax cuts. They do not seem to be effective any more, either. There are a variety of reasons for this, but I shall not enlarge upon them at this time. I am simply pointing out that two of the major engines of economic growth and stimulant in the sixties no longer apply as they did then.
I want to quote the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge who has given this matter some thought. He said on a television show:
It is fairly obvious that some profound change is taking place in our society and governments are no longer able to cope with this kind of change... It's an old society that is dying and there's a whole set of rules that we have to apply now and I don't think anyone is quite sure. In my conversations in the States I was very impressed with some young, bright people who had been brought into the Carter administration for the purpose of rethinking the economics and the kinds of things the government can do, and while they haven't come up with any solutions, all of them are pretty gloomy about the prospects and the abilities of governments to manage the economy in the way that was once thought possible.
If the hon. member is correct, that is a gloomy prescription for us all.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He is not correct.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My hon. friend from Scarborough East (Mr. O'Connell) says he is not correct. I hope my hon. friend is right. But the conclusion we have to draw from his comments, and from what I have said earlier, is that governments will find themselves called upon to experiment with many new techniques, because the old ones are inadequate. New economic conditions are different. The crucial test of a budget, it seems to me, is whether or not the minister has experimented with
The Budget-Mr. Clarke
new techniques and used new techniques in a way likely to stimulate the economy to a meaningful extent. I believe the judgment of the Canadian people, of the provincial premiers, and of this House, will be that the Minister of Finance has done just those things.
I want to take a look at a last point, to run through some things I should like to see the government deal with, and I want to say that these apply not only to the federal government but to the provincial governments as well. Both levels of government suffer from the same symptoms.
First, all governments in Canada have limited fiscal flexibility. The western democracies, and particularly Canada, have all run substantial deficits over past years to meet the widening expectations of their people and, in Canada, to provide jobs for new entrants into the work force. As growth continues, this is not a serious matter. We could cope with it. But growth has slowed down and governments now find themselves in a fiscal bind. It seems clear we are not likely to experience the high growth of the sixties while we are in the process of transforming the economy. This is a consideration with which policy makers will have to deal. The tax policies we have developed at federal and provincial levels were useful during the sixties but are no longer so in the seventies. There has been a preoccupation with equity and redistribution in our tax system. Now I think we shall have to refocus, and look not only at those two principals-
