subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am sorry. The hon. member is quite correct. I have to tell the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Reid) that his time has expired by almost four minutes. I regret that this should have happened. I will now call the next speaker.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I hope hon. members opposite will forgive any sign of self-interest I might have shown in raising that point of order, but I thought the House had probably heard enough from the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Reid).
I think it would be a good idea to start off by mentioning a few of the good points about the budget, because there are a few good points. It is a good news-bad news budget. We have already stated that we agree with the changes made in the research and development field. Write-offs with respect to research and development expenditures will be helpful. It is strange that it has taken Liberal governments 13 years to come back to the idea that we should be encouraging research and development expenditures. It was a Liberal government in 1965 which reversed a policy instituted by the previous Conservative government which allowed the very same 150 per cent write-off for research and development expenditures.

April 13, 1978
The Budget-Mr. Clarke
I am sure that the changes in transportation policy will help the industry, and we welcome those changes.
In the energy field, fast write-offs and other special writeoffs for machinery and equipment and an increase in the depreciation write-off allowance will also be helpful and do their little bit toward getting the economy going again.
Coming from British Columbia, I am disappointed to note that the only mention of the mining industry, which is very important to British Columbia, was a statement by the minister that the government would keep mining provisions under review. Reviews will not help us very much. We need action.
I am sure that many Canadians, particularly older Canadians, will be glad to see that the government has finally bowed to pressure from consumer groups, particularly the Consumers' Association of Canada, supported by members of parliament, particularly members on this side of the House. The government has finally agreed that the rather harsh provisions of the Income Tax Act as they relate to registered retirement plans should be relaxed and that it should not now be mandatory for a Canadian taxpayer to purchase his life annuities before his 71st birthday. The flexibility provided by these new provisions will be welcomed.
The proposed revisions allowing free transfers between spouses for capital gains purposes will be helpful, as will free transfers of incorporated farms to children. However, none of the residents of my riding of Vancouver Quadra are farmers, and many of them will wonder why the government considers that their incorporated family businesses-or unincorporated-are not afforded the same advantage afforded to the farming businesses of Canada's great prairies.
I said there were some good points and I think that pretty well covers them. I would like to dwell for a moment on the bad points of this budget. The effect of the sales tax measure, increased business and so forth which will be created and about which I will be saying more in a few minutes, will amount to a change of less than one-half of one per cent in the unemployment rate. It is clear that we need some program to increase productivity, and in the opinion of hon. members on this side of the House the proposed measures will not do very much. There is absolutely no sign that the government plans any measures to control its expenditures. Without that control the measures contained in the budget will perpetuate the deficits we have had, and debt and interest will mount year after year. It is clear that this budget contains inadequate stimulus for the economy.
When we consider both the good and the bad things in this budget, we might ask whether the government cares about whether its effects will be good or bad. It seems clear that the government does care to a certain extent because I have here a list of the bills introduced by the government since the beginning of this session. Up until the end of February, which covers about four and a half months of this session, 26 items of legislation were introduced. Over five months, that would be an average of five pieces of legislation per month. After February the government felt it might be going to the people and that it should show a little more concern, so in the month

of March 11 pieces of legislation were introduced in the House. In April, up until yesterday, seven pieces of legislation were introduced.
Some might congratulate the government for introducing all that legislation and say that the government is demonstrating forward thinking, but if we look at the list of legislation, we find that the government's forward thinking extends only to the date of a proposed election. For example, what does the government intend to do with Bill C-28, the amendments to the Public Service Staff Relations Act? I think we can safely assume that it will not be debated on the floor of this House before the election and that during the election hon. ministers opposite will traipse around the country telling taxpayers of their intention to pass that legislation, telling them what a great team they are, asking why they should not be re-elected and telling them to forget about the bad things they have been doing for the last ten years.
Another bill which has "election" written all over it is the bill dealing with a public referendum on questions relating to the constitution, Bill C-40. I am sure government ministers will be telling voters what good fellows they are and how well they will do in the next little while. I must confess that hon. members on this side will be doing the same thing in support of our policies but, thankfully, we do not have the record of the government opposite to drag behind us. I can assure hon. members opposite that voters will not forget the last ten years. They have been fooled before by this government, but they will not be fooled again. There are a few items on the list of legislation I have in my hand which indicate what the government will be telling us in any coming election campaign.
As to whether or not the government cares, I would like to refer to the employment tax credit bill which was passed in this House with the co-operation of all opposition parties within one day, which is a very unusual happening. That day was January 26, nearly three months ago, and we are told that there is no sign of the effective date of that tax credit program. The forms are not ready. The government is in disarray, and nobody knows when the program will get started.
The Bank Act is another example of the procedures adopted by this government. The Bank Act expired in 1977. It was extended for, I think, nine months, and it has been extended for another year. Perhaps it will be extended even longer if the House is not in session during the month of March, 1979. What we need is some certainty so that businesses and individuals will know what the government expects of them and they can in an orderly fashion shape their lives and make their own plans. However, the government has presented no measures to stimulate the economy, to make people confident in the government, to stop them from taking their capital and fleeing to other countries to invest, or taking their expertise to other countries. How foolish is it, for example, to have Canadian expertise in building housing for residents of the U.S.A.? Why does the government think that Canadians are saving at a greater rate than ever before? Of course, it is because they do not have confidence that the government will protect the
April 13, 1978

value of the dollar or the value of any investments they might make.
I want to say something about the past policies of the government, since the government likes to defend them so well, to see how they have affected our country recently. Yesterday we saw the cost of living figures rise again. We found that the increase in the Consumer Price Index based on year over year was 8.8 per cent, and we are now in a position where something that cost $100 in 1971 now costs $170.08. The most notorious rise in prices is to be found in food. The index on fruits and vegetables stands at 226.9, and on housing the index for fuel and utilities stands at 221.5-hardly figures which indicate that any of the government's policies have worked. They say: "We have the policies, but you fellows do not have them". We have the proposals and we are expecting very soon to be able to make them into policies. Clearly the policies that have been devised by those fellows opposite have not worked, and there is no way one can say that the figures I have quoted are the result of any kind of good policies.
Yesterday we had cost of living figures. On Tuesday of this week we had the latest figures on unemployment. Total unemployment in Canada stands at 1,045,000, which means a rate of unemployment of 8.6 per cent. Youth unemployment stands at 16.1 per cent. Can the government tell us what great policies they have and how their economic policy has created new jobs in Canada? They say they have created 330,000 new jobs. I say, how nice! It would be wonderful were it not for the fact that there was an increase in the labour force of 432,000. What does that mean? It means that job creation has lagged behind the labour force growth by 102,000 people. Naturally the number of unemployed and the rate are on the increase.
I should point out at the same time that because of the faulty economic policies of the government, not only have the new jobs not kept pace with the new members of the labour force but employment in manufacturing has fallen by some
12,000	through lack of confidence and lack of use of the capacity of industry, thus further aggravating the problem.
What we need is some confidence in the government, as 1 said earlier. How are we going to get it? Let us have a government that is willing to bite the bullet, to use the old expression. Let us have a government that is ready to put the lid on expenses. The President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras), in introducing his estimates this year, took great pride in announcing that the government was cutting down on the rate of increase of government expenditures. You have to stop to think about that statement for a minute because it sounds good, but what he was saying is that the government is not spending as much this year as it spent last year or the year before. All that is coming down is the rate of increase. That might be a step in the right direction if it were not for the fact that the annual growth in the GNP will not be as large as the increase in the rate of growth in government expenditures.
Every time we try to suggest some place where the government could cut down on its expenditures, the government gives
The Budget-Mr. Clarke
us a reason why that cannot be done. They have the facilities over there to determine what the priorities should be, and they are the ones who must make the decision about where they are going to trim. It is impossible to continue spending at an ever increasing rate of deficit. The country will not stand it, the people will not stand it and the economy will not stand it.
The result of the continual policies of overspending and deficit financing by this government over the past ten years can surely be seen in the present low value of our dollar. They call it the floating dollar, and they ask what is wrong with a floating dollar, but a sinking dollar is pretty awful. Today our dollar compared with the U.S. dollar is at a lower point than it has ever been in my lifetime. Not for 45 years has the dollar been as low as it is today. There is no way in which the government can explain away the present level of the dollar compared with the U.S. dollar. The present situation does not even reveal the total problem, because we know that the international economic community does not favour the U.S. dollar very much either and that in relation to the currencies in other industrial countries, such as Germany, Switzerland and Japan, both the Canadian and U.S. dollars are in very bad shape. It is the government that is to blame, and I do not know how they will try to explain that away if we go into an election campaign soon.
The national policies which the government is giving us and which do not work have their effect in British Columbia as well. Every time I go to my riding in Vancouver overlooking English Bay I see 15 ships. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) said today there were 24 ships in the harbour. In any event the figure does vary slightly, but I have never seen less than 15 ships at anchor in English Bay waiting to pick up cargoes which this government cannot get to port. Why can they not move the grain? We do not know. A few years ago they told farmers not to grow more grain because there was too much. Then they turned around and said they needed all the grain that the farmers can grow. Now that the farmers are growing lots of grain, where is it? The minister responsible for moving it to port is saying that it is being moved at the right levels.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No, at record levels.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I wonder what the growers of that wheat are saying. What about the ships lying at anchor? I am afraid it is my friends on the farms in the prairies and my friends back home in Vancouver Quadra who are paying for the storage of grain and for those ships at anchor in the harbours. What we need is someone who will take the grain from the farmers and arrange to move it in orderly fashion down to where the ships are. The minister is saying they are doing it in orderly fashion, but I ask: who arranged the ships? I ask the minister to answer this question.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am delighted that the hon. member allows me to answer the question because he missed my interjection. I want to ask him whether he recognizes that while there are some ships waiting in Vancouver because of difficulties in getting grain there as well as weather conditions, grain is being

April 13, 1978
The Budget-Mr. Clarke moved at record levels and we are almost certain to get a record level of exports in this country. The difficulties are there because of the fact that, in trying to achieve those record levels, we are pushing the system to the full. The hon. member might reflect back-and I wonder if he knows about it-to February of 1961 when his party was in power and when ships were waiting 28 days. At that time the exports were about half those we are achieving this year.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am glad to be able to answer the minister's question because I need the practice. I realize that what he says is correct, but obviously the minister does not understand my complaint. I am glad that the farmers are producing grain at record levels and I am glad Canada is selling grain at record levels. All I ask is why can the government not get the same rate of ship loading as the rate of grain arrival? What is the point of having ships lying at anchor if the grain is not there, although I admit that it adds to the seascape.
The government is always asking us what we would do. What do we need in this country? We need an economic stimulus, and we have been saying that for a long, long time. The hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) told the government in a very interesting speech yesterday of about one hour's duration, and earlier in another speech of about three and a half hours' duration, quite a few things they should be doing and things we would be doing. The essential thing which the hon. member for York-Simcoe has urged upon the government is meaningful permanent tax cuts. I do not know how it can be said any more clearly than that. There is a minor temporary tax cut in the budget. It is going to be shared with the provinces. In his statement the minister said we needed action on this now. He said:
Any further stimulus should obviously be fast-acting. It should encourage consumer spending, not more spending by government.
I agree with that, but I cannot see how spending will be increased by a reduction in the sales tax of 2 per cent, except for government spending as it will be contributing money to offset the reduction of revenue at the provincial level. People who are spending in Canada will spend their money regardless whether there is a 5 per cent sales tax or a 7 per cent sales tax; that is not where the judgment is made as to whether a person is going to buy.
The hon. Leader of the Opposition made reference to the saving on a purchase of a Cadillac. That is a dramatic example. Not many Cadillacs are sold. Certainly on a large purchase like that, there will be a large saving. We are talking about everyday spenders, people who are spending money on essentials. We are not referring to the purchase of food, because that is tax free. We are referring to the other things they are required to buy in their ordinary lives. This kind of stimulation of the economy will not have a permanent effect.
It is asked, what can be done to balance the budget? When a $2 billion tax cut has been given away, it is necessary to increase the revenues on the other side and/or reduce expenditures. There are only two sides to a balance sheet, simple

debits and credits. Because I am an accountant, perhaps I understand it better than others. If credits are to be reduced by giving tax cuts, then we must increase our revenues. We could put a goodly number of those 1,045,000 unemployed people to work. We know there is an 18 per cent under productivity factor in our economy and our productive facilities. If those people are put to work, instead of contributing to the $2 billion deficit in the unemployment insurance account, they will become taxpayers and will contribute to the general revenue of the country. That money does not just go out once and end up there. There is a multiplier in the economy of Canada. When $2 billion is sent out into the economy, it is spent time and time again. That creates more jobs because there are more demands, needs and so on. I am not suggesting any funny money theory when I express that proposal, but it should be obvious to anyone who has studied the economy that it works in that manner. A step in the right direction would be to stop overspending in the unemployment insurance account by putting people back to work.
Many years ago in the United States when there was a tremendous tax cut of $11 billion, at the end of the fiscal year when the revenues were totalled up it was found that revenues were exactly the same because additional taxes paid by the citizens of that country had filled the gap of the $11 billion tax cut.
The Leader of the Opposition referred to some of the policies of our party. I do not think I need to repeat them. We heard the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Reid) say that he did not understand or agree with what the hon. Leader of the Opposition said. That hon. member seemed to think the rules had changed and therefore it is all right for the government to overspend, have huge deficits and so on. Also he indicated that the government was not at fault, that circumstances had changed. We cannot agree with that and Canadians will not agree with that. They want measures to get Canada working again.
We require a little honesty from the government. I should like to remind hon. members opposite about some of their campaign promises made four years ago. How can people have any confidence in a government like that? A promise was made to Toronto regarding a $30 million waterfront park. Perhaps that won a lot of votes, even a few seats in that area. I wonder if the people of Toronto will think of the park which they did not receive when the next election rolls around. What about the statements of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in 1974 during the same election campaign, when he campaigned against controls and 15 months later instituted a lengthy program of controls, which hopefully we will start to get out of tomorrow? Another 1974 campaign promise was that there would be aid to cities for rapid transit. I have been to at least half a dozen cities as a member of a special committee sent out by my party since the 1974 election. We find all across the country that every promise to cities of aid for rapid transit has been broken. How can we have confidence if the government behaves this way, overspends, breaks promises and does not do what it indicated it would do?
April 13, 1978

The leader of my party said it well today. Perhaps he said it somewhat better once or twice in other forums. In the remaining minute or two, I should like to refer to the five points he mentioned. Stop hiring in the federal public service. It is not that we are going to kick anyone out, nor that we think the public service is not doing a good job, but we think the public service has too many employees. They are tripping over themselves. For three years we would impose a freeze on hiring by the public service, and by normal attrition that will save
60,000	jobs at the end of that period.
Also my leader said we should turn back to the private sector Crown corporations like Petro-Can, Eldorado Nuclear Ltd. and Northern Transportation Ltd. There is an enormous amount of money involved in these Crown corporations, most of which do badly. Many of them no longer need the comfort of being owned by the government. They could be and should be turned back to the private sector.
Cutting back on federal regulations is another important point, especially in the manufacturing and mining industries. In particular, today small business is facing difficulties. With regard to cutting down on unnecessary government advertising and consulting, it is well known that the public service uses consultants or contract workers to circumvent the man-year limitations which are put on it. The most important point is the strengthening of parliament's power to control spending by introducing sunset laws and restoring parliamentary control of estimates.
The estimates will be ordered out in a few days. The possible consideration which can be given to the estimates in committee is appalling. The second report of the Standing Committee on Public Accounts was tabled in the House this week. It shows many of the problems regarding the estimates, particularly those of Crown corporations.
I have referred to the unemployment numbers in general. I have some notes regarding the effect on British Columbia, but I see my time has expired.

speakeroldname: Hon. Alastair Gillespie (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on entering the debate this evening I want to concentrate on a number of what I think are very important aspects of Canadian life, the budget and the economy. In particular, I want to show how some of the economic measures in the budget reinforce Canadian energy policy, and how Canadian energy policy reinforces Canadian economic security.
The Budget-Mr. Gillespie
Future economic security is going to depend upon the energy decisions we take now, and how we take them. It is going to depend upon the ability of the federal government to work with the provinces and to take decisions with those provinces. I hope to show in the course of my remarks the kind of progress we have made in this country toward that objective of taking big decisions now, and taking them in co-operation and conjunction with the provinces.
I should like to go back a little bit, about four years ago to January, 1974, when the OPEC nations raised the price of oil. Oil represents the single most important energy source in this world, and the OPEC nations raised the price of oil by four times. The economies of the western world have never been the same since.
Almost immediately the g.n.p. growth and the economies of the western world slowed down, prices rose, inflation became endemic, unemployment increased. The Canadian economy was no different from any other. It too was affected, notwithstanding the fact that our economy depends more than most other nations on export sales. For close to one half of all the goods produced in Canada are exported. To put it another way, close to one half of the goods we produce depends upon the health of economies outside Canada to purchase Canadian production.
The Canadian economy has suffered notwithstanding that fact, but it suffered less, not more, than the economies of other countries. I believe our experience with the performance of the Canadian economy, where it has in effect, in terms of g.n.p. growth, outperformed by a factor of two the OECD countries since 1973, is very significant. Equally, I believe the fact that since that massive price increase we have had less inflation than the OECD rate of inflation is also a considerable achievement as far as Canada is concerned.
To listen to members of the opposition and their leader one would think they had not read the figures. Has anyone in this House heard the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) recognize the importance of that Canadian achievement against that kind of international background? He has been silent on that.
The other important aspect of that OPEC oil price increase is the fact that it involved a massive transfer of resources from the consuming nations to the producing nations-from the western world to the OPEC nations. Again, Canada was no exception. But has the Leader of the Opposition addressed himself to this central fact of international life? Has he addressed himself to this central fact of the international economy? No, he has avoided it, as he has avoided virtually all the central facts with respect to the international situation. I listened very carefully and he did not once recognize the interdependence of the international trading system. He has not recognized that the health of the Canadian mining industry depends on the health of the consuming economies of the countries that buy Canadian mining products. The Leader of the Opposition has a very large blind spot. Other people, less

April 13, 1978
The Budget-Mr. Gillespie
kindly disposed, would ask why the Leader of the Opposition sells Canada short.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Because of the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canada's oil import bill was just a fraction over $1 billion in 1973. Last year it was about $3.5 billion. Had it not been for the extension of the pipeline from Sarnia to Montreal, our oil import bill would be running at about $5 billion per year.
Since 1974 the United States has had the same problem- indeed, a gigantic hemorrhage might be the way to describe it. Before the OPEC increase the oil import bill in the United States was around $7.5 billion per year. Last year it was well over $40 billion. The jump in the value of oil imports for Canada has hurt the Canadian balance of payments, but for the United States it has been a disaster. That $41 billion-plus for oil imports by the United States has affected the value of United States currency in world markets. The United States secretary of the treasury cites this as a major reason for the fall of the U.S. dollar. Unfortunately, it has also contributed to the decline of the Canadian dollar. International experts would ask, when the Canadian economy is so dependent on the United States, why would we not expect an adverse effect on the value of the Canadian dollar?
There was another important message that the OPEC nations conveyed. The first message was that the era of cheap energy was over. The second message was more ominous. They said, "Don't count on us for your future energy supplies." Some of the OPEC nations tightened the tourniquet on the life blood of the western world. I refer to the Arab OPEC nations which cut off a number of their customers, including the United States. That action underscored the position of the OPEC nations and the vulnerability of the economies of the western world. That message, "Don't count on us for your future energy supplies," has been restated many times.
It is against that background that Canadian energy policy has been developed. Two years ago we set forth as the objective of Canadian energy policy to reduce our dependence on foreign oil imports. We put a strategy in place to bring that objective about. The strategy had three basic elements. First came effective conservation measures. There were two others, both of which are part of the replacement. The first is to find substitute kinds of energy indigenous to Canada to replace foreign imports. I am referring, of course, to natural gas, coal, nuclear, hydro, tidal power and other renewable forms. The third main element was to develop our own indigenous supplies of oil, particularly the non-conventional sources-the tar sands and the heavy oils of western Canada.
I believe that we have made a good deal of progress in implementing this strategy. Let us consider conservation. Last year, for example, our record was roughly a 3.3 per cent annual rate of growth, which was perhaps close to one-half of what it had been prior to the energy crisis caused by the OPEC nations in 1973-74 and on the target which we set of less 3.5 per cent annual rate of growth, a target which we hope

to be able to reduce to 2 per cent on an average in the 1980's and hopefully, eventually, to a zero rate of growth per capita.
The International Energy Agency has commented on the Canadian conservation program and described it as one of the best conceived and most comprehensive energy conservation programs in the world. They have, however, criticized one aspect of our policy on conservation because our oil prices have not risen to the international price. They have argued that if we had moved our prices up faster we could have reinforced Canadian conservation objectives. We recognize the merits of that argument. Clearly a faster and higher price would have had a beneficial effect on conservation, but in Canada we tried to balance the conservation objective with another, which is to maintain economic activity, to maintain the competitive advantage of Canadian companies and to sustain the employment and job-creating atmosphere in this country.
I think the record will show that we have been successful in this. At the present time we have met our energy conservation target, but more than that we have more exploratory and development drilling in western Canada than ever. There is not one spare drilling rig available. At the same time, there are more people employed in Canada then there were a year ago-
330,000	more.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Did the Leader of the Opposition once mention that there are 330,000 more Canadians at work in this country? Did he once suggest that this country was moving ahead of other nations? Did he once refer to the dynamism which would provide 330,000 jobs in one year? I listened very carefully, Mr. Speaker, and he implied the reverse-that there were fewer people at work in this country than a year ago.
I believe we have made a lot of progress on the second thrust of our energy strategy, which would use every indigenous source of energy to replace foreign oil imports. I believe we have been able to do it because we have been able to work out with the provinces a co-operative approach to the development of our massive energy resources. Was there one moment when the Leader of the Opposition suggested that the Canadian government had been successful in working out massive projects? He once talked about federal-provincial co-operation, but he does not now.
One is left with the impression that he does not want to draw attention to the successes of the federal government in working out co-operatively massive projects and an economic plan for this country. He does not want to draw attention to the success of the first ministers' conference. He does not want to draw attention to the fact that the major budget provision of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) with respect to the sales tax arrangement was worked out co-operatively with the provinces. He does not want to draw attention to the fact that
April 13, 1978

many of the major energy projects, which I am going to mention, have been worked out co-operatively with the provincial governments.
He does not want to talk about the maritime energy corporation, a corporation which, as the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield) knows, offers the people of the maritimes an opportunity they have never had before, an opportunity to work together with the federal government to bring on massive new projects which by themselves they could not afford. For example, an integrated electrical grid for the maritimes which people have talked about for years can now be a reality. We have agreement on a maritime energy corporation. We have an agreement with respect to the terms of reference, the operating and planning of an integrated maritime electrical system, the management, financing and construction of new generation and transmission facilities, the buying of power and the selling of surplus power. I believe that this particular corporation offers the people of the maritimes an opportunity to be sure of getting the power they need at the lowest possible cost.
The decision of the maritime premiers and the federal government to move forward with phase II of the Bay of Fundy tidal power project is yet another example of the kind of federal-provincial co-operation that I am talking about, but not what the Leader of the Opposition is talking about. He is not talking about these things to the Canadian people because he recognizes them as strengths, as successes of the federal Liberal government.
He has not referred to the conservation and the renewable energy projects we have worked out with the province of Prince Edward Island. He has not talked about the exciting new Cape Breton Island coal mine development project for the Donkin mine. He has not talked about the agreement with the province of Newfoundland for the creation of the lower Churchill Falls development corporation to develop the massive potential of the lower Churchill Falls, the 2,000 megawatts of power which is spilling out over the rocks and into the sea. He has not talked about that, Mr. Speaker, because he does not want to draw attention to yet another successful enterprise of the federal government with the provinces.
There are a number of other major projects which will assist Canadians to become less dependent on foreign oil. I am referring to the Canada/U.S. development of the emergency oil storage in Wabana, Newfoundland and in Canso, Nova Scotia, presently before our two governments. As well I am referring to the Petro-Canada activity off the Nova Scotian shelf and off the shores of Labrador. He has not talked about those Petro-Canada activities and he has not talked about the fact that, if it was not for the leadership of Petro-Canada, one would not see the kind of study that is taking place right now in Quebec and the maritimes with respect to moving western gas to the maritimes.
Hon. members have not heard from the Leader of the Opposition about the liquefied natural gas projects which have been developing in the minds of those in charge of Trans-
The Budget-Mr. Gillespie
Canada Pipelines and Petro-Canada, projects which could move high Arctic natural gas to the east coast, perhaps through the terminal at Saint John, New Brunswick at Lor-neterm, or perhaps through another terminal at Canso.
Hon. members have not heard about these projects because the Leader of the Opposition wants to abolish Petro-Canada. That is what he has told the Canadian people.

April 13, 1978
The Budget-Mr. Gillespie
Nuclear energy has to be one of the major options for Canada in reducing our dependence on foreign oil. That is not something which the Conservative party have yet addressed themselves to.
I could go on about exploration and drilling in the high Arctic, the importance of the polar gas operation and Petro-Canada's position in that. speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources

speechtext:
I would like to deal with the third thrust of our energy strategy, the development of our own indigenous resources. Hon. members will be aware that the government has presented to parliament Bill C-19, which is presently before the House and awaiting third and final reading. Bill C-19 would provide authority for the government to offer international prices for the production of tar sands projects and heavy oil projects. That represents a truly massive opportunity for Canadians. The budget has introduced a number of very important measures aimed at helping to provide the fiscal climate or regime whereby these massive projects will be undertaken. This fiscal regime will have to be worked out and negotiated with the provinces concerned.
In addition to the incentives in the budget 1 have referred to, the depletion incentives, the fact we will move to world prices for these new products and the other new incentives which the Minister of Finance referred to, there are a number of important measures which I should announce this evening. One has to do with the federal government's decision to meet the costs of moving domestic crude oil through the interprovincial pipeline between Toronto and Montreal.
Secondly, to make full use of this pipeline, to which I referred earlier, I believe we should increase the throughput of that pipeline from 250,000 barrels a day to 350,000 barrels a day. Such an increase of roughly 100,000 barrels daily would be the equivalent in balance of payments terms of a saving of $500 million a year. That is a truly significant saving in terms of balance of payments. To this end, I have initiated discussions with the Alberta government and the Interprovincial pipeline.
Hon. members will agree that the government has taken several important and very necessary steps to encourage expansion of non-conventional oil production. However, the federal government cannot do everything. I think this is recognized by the producing provinces. Alberta has already acted to provide heavy oil producers with alternative royalty incentives. It is my hope that Alberta and Saskatchewan will announce in the very near future measures they are prepared to take so that the total fiscal regime, including income tax and royalties, will lead without doubt to commercial development of these massive oil reserves in western Canada.
I believe the governments of Saskatchewan and Alberta are sympathetic to our objectives. In general, they appear willing to adjust their own royalty regime to provide the further incentives which are absolutely necessary if these projects are to go forward. Shell Oil has already announced its interest in a consortium. Imperial Oil has announced their interest. There have been discussions with respect to the Pacific petroleum group and another group headed up by Husky. We have also been-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: This is not new. It has been going on for years.

speechtext: Yes, Mr. Speaker, but we are now waiting to hear from the provincial governments as to what royalty changes they are prepared to make. I am confident that in the spirit we have been able to work out these other arrangements we will also be able to work out the new fiscal regime which will bring on the kind of production we are looking for. I hope we will be successful in being able to produce close to one million barrels a day from the tar sands and heavy oils of western Canada by 1990.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

These projects in Canada are not going to be developed by negative attitudes, by people who only look at the

problems, who do not build a sense of achievement in Canadians, people who would try to deflect Canadian opinion away from the kind of opportunities which are in Canada.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would not want to miss the opportunity to make a few remarks on this mini-budget, because, in my opinion, that is exactly what it is. It would seem that the first part was presented before Christmas and, under pressure, the minister decided to add to it. But I do not think that this budget will impress economists, experts and Canadians.
Unfortunately I had to be absent from the House a few days as I was called to an important meeting in my riding last night. I would have wanted to make these remarks sooner, but as this was my nomination meeting, Mr. Speaker, I had to be there and prepare myself for a good fight with my opponent who will be a candidate in the coming election. I heard the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) recall the efforts made by his government and try to justify the proposals put forth by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) as well as the situation which exists today.
He even blamed our leader (Mr. Clark) for not having referred to certain government achievements. In view of the unsatisfactory performance and the shortcomings of this government in virtually all areas, our leader certainly did not have much time left after having noted the many failures of the government in meeting nearly all its objectives. Everyone will recognize that it is our duty to tell the Canadians about the sad performance of the government in its monumental failure to restore our economy. I do not think we can be prevented from doing so, not only in the House, but in all public forums. I think that it is our duty to tell the Canadians how miserably this government has failed to meet its objectives in the last decade especially in the last four years.
I do not understand, Mr. Speaker, how the minister can accuse us of seeing only doom and gloom in view of the present situation concerning unemployment, inflation, and so on. Members on the other side may well ask why we are so pessimistic about the future, and why we seem somewhat negative about the proposals made by the government.
I was listening to a member from Quebec City. He too is worried, but he would like Canadians to accept the unfortunate administration that we have had in the last ten years. But we will have the opportunity to describe our present situation to the people of Quebec City and of other areas of Quebec as well as of the rest of Canada. Monday night, the Minister of Finance seemed quite happy when he delivered his budget speech. In principle, he announced his budget. Perhaps we could ask this question: Why did he wait so long? As I recall, we have been requesting for many months a budget which could correct in part, or at least satisfactorily, the present situation.
The highlights of this budget show that unemployment and inflation have reached their highest level, while the dollar is at its lowest level. This bears out a forecast made a long time ago and according to which the deficit would reach $11 billion. This is not what we were told six or seven months ago. They were then trying to convince us that the deficit would not be over $6, $7, or $8 billion. About four months ago, one of my colleagues, our financial critic, predicted a deficit of over $10 billion.
Still our friends opposite accuse us of being prophets of doom, and of being responsible for the lack of confidence shown by Canadian and foreign investors. But we have been saying the truth for the last six months. We were also saying the truth when we reminded the government on many occasions or tried to warn it that Canada was heading toward a lengthy and costly depression.
Those are the highlights of the budget of the Minister of Finance: unemployment has reached a record high, as did inflation, and our dollar is at its lowest. The Minister of Finance argues that our Canadian dollar is still floating, but we believe it is sinking. We are certainly considered as prophets of gloom. But, Mr. Speaker, this is the present situation and we cannot hide it.
I also believe that this $11 billion deficit will certainly not encourage businessmen and that it will rather make them worry about the present situation. The predecessors of the Minister of Finance have already made economic projections. The present Minister of Finance also made his projections. It did not change the situation. And this budget confirms what we have been expecting for several months. But in spite of this, earlier the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources tried to reassure Canadians by telling them that the situation is not too bad.
However, we are blamed for not being willing to endorse those projections without too much discussion. But, Mr. Speaker, how could we trust a government that is responsible for the unemployment of 1,500,000 workers. The Prime Minister told us last week that he had created thousands of jobs. But how would you explain that with such positive results we have four times more unemployed than when the Prime Minister came to power? How would you explain that this government has not been able to plan for new jobs to accommodate new markets and the people who arrive on the labour market every day? The Minister of Finance refused to make sufficient credit available for job creation for students. He knows that is true either in his riding or in mine.
The hon. member for Montmorency is also aware of the difficulties students will experience this summer. If I refer to what has apparently been the experience of the Prime Minister when he was a university student, there is no doubt that he can hardly understand the financial difficulties encountered by our

April 13, 1978

students because he has never had to wonder where the money would come from. It is therefore difficult for him to think that our students will go through financial difficulties. We are perfectly aware that this government is asking us to put our trust in it and will soon ask the Canadian people to trust it, yet the government is indeed responsible for refusing to grant enough funds to create jobs for students. I can see members opposite trying to argue but in each of their ridings the students are in the same predicament as in mine; they are worried because they will not find summer jobs. Mr. Speaker, this same government is asking us to trust it while it is responsible for the 5,000 to 6,000 dairy producers who went out of business during the last two years.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is not true.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am being told that it is not true. But who can pretend that this is not true, Mr. Speaker? Dishonesty becomes obvious. It is clear that the government's poor administration and poor management of the dairy industry has thrown thousands of producers out of business. That same government is asking us to trust it when it refuses to compensate the cost of maintaining provincial police forces in the provinces of Quebec and Ontario, as it has been requested recently. There are no funds, no provision for that in the budget.
We will be asked to trust this government while it is responsible for the deterioration of the textile and footwear industry. Thousands of jobs have been lost because of the passiveness of this government. My friends opposite know that, some members in front of me have experienced serious problems in their own riding because of that and we are going to hide those facts. We should not mention it. This government is responsible for the highest inflation rate we have ever experienced; it is responsible for the declining purchasing power of Canadians; it is responsible for failing to provide sufficient grants for research which might have prevented the closing of plants in our country; it is responsible for the deterioration of our dairy industry and now we are called prophets of gloom because we have reasons, I believe, to blame the government for its inertia and its lack of success in finding the necessary solutions, Mr. Speaker.
We have been making proposals for quite a while, Mr. Speaker. I would also like to point out an important aspect of the budget where my friends from Quebec have a major responsibility as regards the proposal which was made by the Minister of Finance and which is rejected by the Quebec government.
The Minister of Finance rejects the proposal made by the Quebec minister and at the same time opposes the will of Quebecers, and not only of the Quebec government, since in principle the opposition parties of the Union Nationale or the Quebec Liberal Party have agreed on the position and the request of the Quebec government, and that is important. I
The Budget-Mr. La Salle
suggest that is the most significant factor. The National Assembly has unanimously requested the Minister of Finance to answer affirmatively to the proposal of the Quebec government which is asking for only one thing-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And your leader, what does he think about it?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
They are not asking for one cent more from the federal government. They are simply asking that Quebec be allowed to use the same amount of money as befit the realities and the needs of the province and the Quebec government is prepared to suggest any province which would like to get the same advantages. Obviously Quebec would not object to any other province getting the same advantages.
Something I find repulsive, something I feel is a scandal is the attitude of our members from Quebec on that question. I heard over the radio this evening a report I hope is true. The report on TV was that a number of members from the Quebec Liberal caucus were meeting this evening to oppose the decision or position taken by the Minister of Finance. I hope this is true, I hope I am not the only one of this side to understand Quebec's true interests.
There are 60 Quebec members on the other side, and their silence this afternoon is the worst act of betrayal I have ever witnessed in this House in respect of a highly legitimate request from the Quebec government, which the Minister of Finance apparently is refusing. I hope my friends opposite will take this opportunity to rise and take a stand in favour of Quebec's request. It is certainly not at odds with the rest of Canada. And when apparently the Minister of Finance is not in a position to accept such a proposal, he must be subject to unknown pressures. He is betraying his mandate to respond to his province's true interests, as every member has a responsibility to do so. If this measure that will not cost Canada one cent more could be implemented in a fashion more germane to Quebec's vital interests, it would allow Quebecers to take advantage of the 8 per cent tax reduction in vital areas, products of almost daily consumption. I feel this would meet the legitimate aspirations of Quebecers. In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I call on people in authority on the government's side, Quebec members who took a commitment in 1974, who have been promising the province of Quebec these last ten years that if the federal government were represented in large numbers by Quebecers, the province would derive additional benefits. God knows what has been happening during those last ten years. After so many requests were turned down, and not only since 1976 because Mr. Bourassa also faced refusals from the same government, as much as Mr. Johnson, Mr. Bertrand and Mr. Lesage. Since they are now in power-

speechtext:

speechtext:
When I finish my remarks, Mr. Speaker, I will accept any question. I conclude, Mr. Speaker, because the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) has asked me to end my remarks in order to leave him the floor. In conclusion I appeal to my friends from Quebec, Mr. Speaker, I ask my friends from the province of Quebec to have the guts to urge the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) to respect the interest of his own province. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I believe it is important to underline this fact because the Minister of Finance did not consult the provinces sufficiently.
