However, if the federal government has $1 billion available to increase the purchasing power of Canadians, why did he not call on the premiers or the finance ministers to ask them how they wanted to spend this money-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The Quebec premier left!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is not what this government usually does. If this government wants to make a decision, it tells the provinces: Take it or leave it. That is the attitude of this government and that is the problem. For our part, we believe in consultation to correct the situation. I have been asked what should be done to achieve that. We believe that in a healthy and viable federal state, it is important to allow the provinces to take part in the major national decisions. We all recognize that the provinces must participate fully and truly in the making of the major national decisions and that this would eliminate our present problems, including that raised in the House today. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I hope that the Minister of Finance will reflect tonight about the request made by the Quebec government and approved, as I said before, by the opposition parties.
The measure proposed by Quebec is so reasonable, timely, desired and wanted by the people that it has been approved unanimously by the government. The acting leader of the Liberal party and the leader of the official opposition stated it was sound federalism. The colleagues, the friends of members opposite in Quebec consider that co-operating with this proposition is sound federalism.
I notice that the hon. member for Bonaventure-Iles-de-la-Madeleine (Mr. Bechard) does not agree with me, and that is a scandal. Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, I see that some of my colleagues from Quebec do not care for the vital interests of their province, and in a few days they will ask the voters in Quebec to trust them when they have been betraying them so

blatantly as they are doing today, when they have lied to them for ten years, they have forgotten their promises, and they have shown no respect for their own constituents. I hope this matter will be reconsidered, Mr. Speaker, that reason will prevail and that the requests and the interests of our province will be paid more consideration.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Now that the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle) is through with his speech, I would like to know if he would answer one question. And before I ask my question, I would like to say, Mr. Speaker, that the reason why the Progressive Conservative party has so few French Canadian members in Quebec is quite obvious after listening to such rubbish inspired by such intellectual dishonesty. Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Joliette said that since the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has been in office, his province did not receive anything. I would like to give one example: I would like to ask him if he could tell the House the percentage increase in equalization since 1968?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in no way did I suggest the government did nothing. In my opening remarks I stated the minister had stressed actions and accomplishments. What I said is that was done too late. This is what I said. When the hon. member for Bonaventure-Iles-de-la-Madeleine accuses me of being intellectually dishonest, I must tell him I only stated the government's poor performance and failures. The hon. member for Bonaventure-lles-de-la-Madeleine among others is objecting. He is only proving he is dishonest because he knows he is refusing once more, as so many other Quebecers, to support Quebec's position and best interests.
I am truly ashamed at that member's behaviour and certainly I cannot accept his accusations, because every time I rose in this House I endeavoured to enhance our responsibilities as members in this House. I feel therefore that the question or the interjection of the hon. member for Bona venture-Iles-de-la-Madeleine is quite malicious, and much more dishonest than anything I may have said since the beginning of my remarks.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I was right in suggesting he is dishonest, because he did not even answer my question.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I answer intelligent questions only.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order, please. I suggest that both hon. members are now getting into a debate.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to participate in this debate I want to begin by spending a few moments discussing the words of wisdom we heard today from the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) and the words of wisdom we heard from the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens), who led off the debate for the official opposition a couple of days ago. As part of his prescription for what
April 13, 1978

ails the government the hon. member for York-Simcoe suggested, among other things, that a Conservative government would reduce the size of the public service by attrition, would stop filling vacancies in the public service, and over a period of three years would reduce the public service by between 50,000 and 60,000 people. Of course, the impression he created was that this would be done very gradually and in a way that nobody would be hurt.
Those words had an oddly reminiscent sound. It seemed to me I had heard them somewhere before. I hear my colleague the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) say "in 1930". No. Mr. Speaker, I heard them just a few months ago, within the last year. I concentrated and suddenly I realized that in Manitoba we heard all that talk last year in August, September and October. The leader of the official opposition, the present Conservative premier of Manitoba, was telling the people of Manitoba just that kind of thing. One Conservative candidate in that provincial election was approached by a civil servant who said to him: "I am concerned, I am not happy with the NDP government. I have been thinking about voting Conservative but the way the leader of your party talks, it sounds to me as if there are going to be wholesale lay-offs of civil servants". So this candidate thought that he should find out what the party position was and he wrote a letter to the then leader of the opposition, Mr. Lyon, who sent him a letter which he authorized him to use in his campaign, and which was used in the campaign, in which he said that the Conservative party of Manitoba believed that the civil service in that province could be made more efficient and could be slimmed down, but that this would be done by attrition and that certainly no permanent employee would be laid off. The Conservative party won the election and Mr. Lyon is the premier of Manitoba. He has been in office for six months, and between 1,000 and 2,000 civil servants have been laid off in that time.
However, I want to talk for a few minutes not just about the people who were laid off but to put on the record what that Conservative government has done. I think members of the House and the people of Canada can get an idea of what the Conservative party of Canada mean when they talk about restraint and about cutting the expenditures of government. They can see what happened in Manitoba in six shorts months.
Before the NDP formed the government in Manitoba, the total number of senior citizens' housing units and public housing units, despite the fact the federal government for many years has paid 50 per cent or more of the cost of building those units, amounted to less than 1,000. That is the total which was built during the time of the Liberal government and the Progressive Conservative government. During the eight years in which the NDP formed the government, 12,000 housing units were built for senior citizens and for people who could not afford to buy or rent their own homes. The housing units are beautiful. Senior citizens who have no income except their old age pensions qualify for efficiency apartments. That program applied to senior citizens who
The Budget-Mr. Orlikow
received old age pension payments of $50 a month or less. That program has been discontinued, with no exception. The public housing unit program has been discontinued as well.
The provincial government inaugurated, with the federal government assisting in financing, a very impressive home repairs program for senior citizens who needed modest repairs to their electrical systems, plumbing systems or foundations. They were entitled to a loan, a grant, or a combination of the two, from the governments in order to have their homes repaired. Some 20,000 homes were repaired when the NDP was in power. That program has been stopped as well.
The government funded a school nutrition program in the core area of the city of Winnipeg. In that area there are a large number of students who come from new immigrant homes and native families. That program has been discontinued.
The universities have been told that the money they will get in this coming year will be not more that 2.6 per cent over what they received last year. That means a decrease in funding for the universities in Manitoba of approximately 6 per cent. The students' fees were increased by 20 per cent in one year as well. The grants to municipalities were very drastically pruned, so that the municipal taxes in Winnipeg, as well as other cities and towns in Manitoba, will go up between $75 and $125 this year.
During the last few years I have not used a car in Ottawa. I have used the public transit system. I have seen the ticket price go up from 25 cents in 1974 to 55 cents, or seven tickets for $3, in the three and a half years since the 1974 election. Until approximately two weeks ago, the fare in Winnipeg was 25 cents a ticket, with the provincial government picking up 50 per cent of the deficit incurred by the Winnipeg transit system. The new provincial government in Manitoba refused to increase its contribution, so the cost of a fare has risen from 25 cents to 35 cents, which is an increase of 40 per cent in one year.
The fees for people in nursing homes have been increased. Despite the promises made before and since the election by Mr. Lyon, today user fees were announced for elderly persons in acute care beds in hospitals. There are old people and sick people in Manitoba who should be in senior citizens' housing projects or nursing homes. Despite the job the former government did in building such facilities, there is still a shortage, as there is in most parts of Canada. There are people who have gone into hospital with acute illnesses and who are now ready to leave the hospital but cannot because there is no place for them to go. These are the people who are to be charged a fee.
Perhaps some of my friends, particularly my Conservative friends, will say that I am exaggerating. I should like to quote from a news story which appeared in the April 11, 1978 edition of the Winnipeg Free Press. Its headline is: "Take 3.2 per cent cut to avoid lay-offs, hospital asks". It reads as follows:
Victoria General Hospital is asking its employees to accept a 3.2 per cent wage cut to avoid lay-offs.
80033 - 71V2

April 13, 1978
The Budget-Mr. Orlikow
The hospital told four unions late last week the province's 2.9 per cent limit in additional operating funds this year means substantial lay-offs otherwise.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What about collective bargaining?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
They have collective bargaining. They finalized an agreement which gave them a 6 per cent increase. It was the maximum permitted under the guidelines of the anti-inflation legislation. The hospital is acting under the instructions or direction of the new government. Since it can only get an increase in operating grants of 2.9 per cent from the province, the hospital must react in the only way it can. It has told the employees either to take a cut in wages or people will be laid off. Not only does that result in more unemployment, it means a drastic cut in the standard of hospital care in the province of Manitoba.
When hon. members of the official opposition talk about the government being wasteful, about a freeze in the number of public servants, slimming down the public service by not filling vacancies when they occur and so on, they are talking about a very substantial reduction in the services which are provided by the federal government to Canadians, similar to what happened to the people of Manitoba since the Conservative government was elected provincially there.
Now I should like to turn to the budget which was placed before parliament a few nights ago by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien). We have been given a part-time budget to meet the needs of a spring election. That is how the budget speech was described virtually by every newspaper, radio station and television station. Now we are faced with a situation such as we have not seen since prior to World War II, such as we have not seen since the great depression of the thirties. For the first time in the history of Canada, for three months running, there are more than one million unemployed people. For the month of March, the last month for which we have figures, according to Statistics Canada the official figure is 1,047,000 unemployed people. That is an increase of more than 100,000 people over the same month last year. On a seasonally adjusted basis, that represents 8.6 per cent of our labour force.
There is not a member of parliament who does not realize that several hundred thousand people are unemployed but are not counted. Our estimate is that 500,000 people are in such a position. In order to be counted you must be actively looking for work. There are many areas in this country, such as in Newfoundland, Cape Breton Island and the Inter Lake District of Manitoba near my constituency, where there are no jobs and have been none for several years, and there is no real point in someone who is unemployed there looking for work.
The Minister said the other night in his budget speech that it is not possible to provide jobs for everybody in Canada who wants to work. He trotted out some stale figures and prided himself on the jobs that have been created in Canada. It is true we have more people employed than ever before in Canada, but that is cold comfort to the more than one million people unemployed at this time.

In the years I have been here I suppose I have heard one hundred or more speeches at various times damning trade unions because they are too demanding and because sometimes they call a strike. Many of those spokesmen have suggested that the people do not want to work. How many of us have asked ourselves what one million unemployed people really means?
Every day we have one million people unemployed we lose one million days of productive work. One economist has calculated that between 1974 and 1978 we have lost some $20 billion in lost production because of unemployment, and that is unemployment over and above the 3.5 per cent to 4 per cent which has always been taken as full employment. Every three and a half days we have one million unemployed we lose more than we lost during all the strikes in Canada last year. Every twelve working days we lose more through unemployment than we lost in total to strikes in 1976. Members will remember how the newspaper editorial writers talked about the terrible things unions were doing to this country by going on strike.
Almost 40 per cent of the unemployed today are young people between the ages of 15 and 24 years. These are among the best educated and trained young people this country has ever had. We have spent hundreds of millions of dollars in our school systems, our community colleges, our technical institutions and our universities training our young people, and now they find there are no jobs. Our young people are graduating as teachers, as social workers, as engineers and in almost every field, but are being told not only that there are no jobs, but in such a way it seems as though it is their fault they have so much training. What could be more cynical or more cruel than that?
The Minister of Finance interjected during the speech of the Leader of the Official Opposition this afternoon: "Who is C. D. Howe?" I do not know whether he was joking or in fact did not know. For the information of the minister, C. D. Howe was probably the most important cabinet minister in this country during World War II. He was in charge of war production and virtually everything that mattered. In 1945 when the war ended he was the minister of reconstruction. I think in April of that year he tabled on behalf of the then Liberal government a white paper on reconstruction in which he said on behalf of the government that a Liberal government would not be satisfied with anything but full employment. He did not refer to a "large number employed", or to "most people", or to 85 per cent, 90 per cent or 95 per cent, or to "people who want to work"; he referred to "full employment". That is what that Liberal cabinet minister, who really was the most important minister during and after the war, had to say about what the Liberal party felt in 1945. This Liberal government of 1978 could take a lesson from that Liberal government of 1945.
Not only did we get the latest unemployment figures this week showing more than one million unemployed, we got the latest figures on the cost of living. Lo and behold, in spite of all the huffing and puffing of this government, in spite of lectures ad nauseam to the people of Canada by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of Finance, and in spite of
April 13, 1978

that whole bureaucratic jungle of the Anti-Inflation Board, the cost of living in one month jumped by 1.1 per cent, and for the whole year, from March 1977 to March 1978, the cost of living rose by 8.8 per cent. This is in the third year of the so-called anti-inflation program.
We get lectures from the Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance and occasionally from the chairman of the Anti-Inflation Board in which they have told us that if we exclude fuel prices and food prices we are right on target, just as though the people could live without paying for heat and power and buying food. We are told we are on target and doing better than most countries, but occasionally even this government has to tell the truth.
Frequently when we read about some of the terrible things that happen in the United States, such as Watergate and other things a super power like the United States can become involved in, we like to think that cannot happen in Canada because we are better than they. However, there are some things the United States has that we do not have, and one of those things is a securities and exchange commission.
If any corporation, individual or government wants to borrow money by selling bonds in the United States, they must first file a prospectus with the securities and exchange commission. Unfortunately we do not have similar legislation in Canada and we do not have such a commission. If you want to sell bonds in the United States you must go to the securities and exchange commission and explain what you are trying to do, what collateral you have, what your assets are, and so on. Fortunately or unfortunately, depending on how you look at it, the United States government requires this kind of information to be made public. People in Canada who do not think this kind of information should be made public, such as the President of the CNR, would think this is unfortunate, and he in fact does think it is unfortunate.
When the Government of Canada went to the United States recently to sell bonds they had to file a prospectus with the securities and exchange commission there. I hear the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Hogan) say that was one of the first times ever. In our view it is fortunate they did because the prospectus has been published. Let me put on record what this great Liberal government, which tells us that inflation is under control, is on target and so on, put in their prospectus. In an article in the Montreal Gazette of April 12, Don McGillivray quotes from the prospectus as follows and adds his comments:
"Specific inflation targets, as measured by the consumer price index, were set"-
This refers to the Anti-Inflation Board and the guidelines.
-"at 8 per cent, 6 per cent and 4 per cent for the first, second and third program years ending in October 1976, 1977 and 1978, respectively. During the first program year, the rate of price increase was 6.2 per cent, but in the second year was 8.8 per cent."
No nonsense there about the 6 per cent target for this year or about the 'underlying' rate of inflation, minus food and energy prices, being within last
The Budget-Mr. Hees
year's guideline. The government evidently felt it had to level with foreign investors but could snow Canadians a little.
That is the situation, Mr. Speaker. Until budget night the Minister of Finance claimed that the rate of inflation for 1978 would be on target at 6 per cent. That in itself was a misstatement of the original target, because this is the third year of the program and the rate should have been 4 per cent. We will give the minister some leeway, however. He was saying that the rate of inflation should have been 6 per cent for this year, although he knows that devaluation of the dollar means substantial increases in the price of everything. Increases are particularly sharp in the price of all the food we import, which means virtually all vegetables in winter and all fruit in a large part of the year.
The minister knew that the government is committed to regular increases in the price of oil and natural gas until, within the next three or four years, they reach the international price. That means in the coming year at least two increases of $1.00 per barrel of oil and similar increases for natural gas. Those two increases alone will drive the cost of living up by about 2.5 per cent. When the minister spoke about a 6 per cent inflation target on Monday night, he must have known that it was in fact going to be substantially more. You can only bluff the people for so long, Mr. Speaker. On Monday night the minister finally admitted that the 6 per cent target for the cost of living increase in 1978 was not feasible and said the increase would be 7 per cent. It is obvious to anyone with the most elementary knowledge of economics that, unless the exchange rate on the Canadian dollar climbs in comparison to the United States dollar, we are facing not a 6 per cent increase in the cost of living or a 7 per cent increase but probably in the neighbourhood of 8 per cent.
We have not yet seen the effects of the things that are happening in the United States, such as the increase in wages won by the coal miners and the increase in prices that the steel companies imposed. These will work their way through the United States economy and will mean a sharp increase in inflation which will be reflected in Canada. As my colleague the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond says, it will be between 8 and 9 per cent. I am sure he is much closer to the truth than the Minister of Finance.
There were some goodies for various interested groups in the budget, but essentially it was a political budget. Sales taxes were cut by 3 per cent for six months. That means that in October when unemployment traditionally begins to climb and the economy needs a boost the cut in sales tax will come off. The minister hopes the cut will find favour with the Canadian people and help his party win the next election, after which they can face the consequences for another four years. I have more confidence in the Canadian people, Mr. Speaker.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order please. I regret to inform the hon. member that his allotted time has expired.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the short time available to me I will try and go over the sad record of this government in the past ten years and judge

April 13, 1978
The Budget-Mr. Hees
just how much support it deserves in the election that is coming up shortly.
Let me take unemployment first. In 1968 there were 375,000 people unemployed; in 1978, there are over one million unemployed, almost triple the number. In 1968 inflation was 4.5 per cent; in 1978 it is 8.7 per cent, triple the rate. The cost of a new NHA house in 1968 was $18,900; today it is $40,500, more than double. The mortgage rate in 1968 was 8 per cent; today it is 1014 per cent, an increase of nearly one-third. In 1968 the current account deficit was $97 million; today it is $4.5 billion, having increased 44 times. In 1968 the trade deficit for manufactured products, the ones that produce the jobs, was $3.1 billion; today it is $11.6 billion, an increase of almost four times.
From these figures it is evident that this is the worst performance ever put forward by a government in the history of this country.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Let me look at who has resigned from this government in protest over the way the economy has been run. The first was Mr. Eric Kierans, economics professor at McGill University, president of the Montreal Stock Exchange and a provincial minister of revenue before he entered the cabinet. Then there was in succession Mr. John Turner and Mr. Donald Macdonald, both of whom served as minister of finance. These three gentlemen resigned because the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) insisted on following an irresponsible socialist line which they could see clearly was leading the country into economic disaster.
Another member of cabinet, Mr. Paul Hellyer, the then deputy prime minister, quit because the Prime Minister refused to bring in a housing program to benefit low income people. That took place, Mr. Speaker, immediately following the Prime Minister's campaign across the country on the program of a just society. What a farce that turned out to be when he took over with a majority after the election!
Let us see who is left running the store. First of all, we have the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) who, in this budget, brought in a sales tax cut which is to expire in six months' time, in the fall when unemployment always starts to rise. This is going to bring about a disastrous slump which, of course, this government does not care about because there is only one purpose in bringing in that measure. That purpose is to tide this government over the election, which is to be called in the next day or so, and that is the only purpose of this tax cut.
Then, Mr. Speaker, we have a departmental study which was produced by the Department of Industry Trade and Commerce entitled "Manufacturing Performance". It states that the manufacturing sector of our economy has lost no less than 80,000 jobs in the last four years. The minister's idea of helping the manufacturing industry of this country is to lower tariffs. He stated that in the House of Commons recently. He said that all tariffs are going to be cut an average of 40 per
[Mr. Hees.)
cent. If under his direction and the direction of this government that proposal is adopted at the GATT negotiations in Geneva today, then later this fall those disastrous tariff cuts, will result in complete disaster for the manufacturing industry in this country and will produce far greater lay-offs than we have seen for a very long time.
This government is going to the country in the next few days with the slogan "Show you care". I have news for the Prime Minister: the people of this country are already adding four words to that slogan which the Prime Minister is going to hear. He will hear these words all over this country in his election campaign, and they are "Get rid of Pierre".

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The obvious alternative to the shambles this government has made of running this economy into the ground is the program of economic competence and responsibility which has been presented in the last two days by the hon. leader of this party and by our financial critic, the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens). This program is a positive program, a national development program which will get this country back on its feet. This is what this country deserves. It will restore the economic performance which the people of Canada deserve to receive from the government which they will have sitting over there, a Conservative government, as soon as the election results are announced on election night.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!
